t: until it has first been moistened... and this is called hechsher. Food must be wetted by a liquid (from the seven liquids listed below) before impurity touches it, and thereby it is rendered susceptible to impurity.
as it says, 'and if water is put on seed'. And the verse continues: 'and any part of their carcass falls on it, it is impure to you.'
and oil. Olive oil.
and honey. Bee honey (but date honey is not considered a liquid, below, halakhah 21).
and they must not be putrid. Spoiled, not fit for anything (Commentary on the Mishnah, Eduyot 2:3; and see below 2:14, 2:21).

that have not reached a third. They have not reached a third of their growth (for the definition of a third of growth in olives see Hilchot Ma'aser 2:5), and therefore the liquids that come out of them are not considered liquids for impurity.
the kosht. A plant from which perfume is extracted.
and the chamam. A strongly scented plant of the ginger family; some explain it is a kind of cinnamon.
and the chief spices. All the fragrant plants (Commentary on the Mishnah, Uktzin 3:5).
and the tiya and the chiltit. Seasoning plants in cold countries (ibid.).
and the pepper. Black pepper.
and the cakes of chariya. Chariya is safflower, and chalot chariya are a part of the plant used for coloring dishes (ibid.).

the shevet. A vegetable (now called dill) that is customarily eaten raw as a dessert at the end of the meal (Commentary on the Mishnah, Uktzin 3:4), or crushed and eaten in a food called kutach (Rashi, Niddah 51b), but it is also used to flavor a dish and then removed from it.

by default, for eating it itself. As long as he has not designated it otherwise, it is meant to be eaten raw, and therefore it becomes impure with the impurity of foods (Commentary on the Mishnah, ibid.).
and if he designated it for the pot. If he explicitly designated it for cooking (Riko, in the second explanation).

and the shevet, once it has given flavor to the pot etc.. This speaks of a shevet he did not designate for the pot; if he put it in the pot anyway, it does not leave its impurity until it gives flavor to the pot and is no longer fit to eat (see ibid.).
and dried figs. Figs.
until they are rendered unfit for human consumption. As with all foods that do not receive impurity in this condition (below 2:14).
the karshinin. A kind of legume (today called bitter vetch) used mainly as animal fodder.
the kor. The soft part at the top of the palm tree that is fit for human consumption.
and if he boiled them and fried them. Boiling is cooking in water and frying is done in oil.
the seeds. The inner grape pits.
and the skins. The outer grape skins. The pits and skins are considered the waste of the fruit (Hilchot Nezirut 5:2).
hard olives and grapes that burst out from under the beam at the time of pressing. Because they are hard they are not squeezed by the beam but are squeezed out.
up to four kavs per kor. As long as the quantity of olives and grapes that burst out is not more than four kavs per kor of produce (about 2.25 percent).
if the amount that burst out was more than this, they receive impurity. In such a quantity they have importance of their own even though they are hard and unfit for pressing.
and if he gathered them for food. He collected them for eating.
the kafniyot. Clusters of dates at the beginning of their growth (Commentary on the Mishnah, Orlah 1:9).
and the pagim. Very small fruits at the beginning of the ripening process.
and the boser. Fruits at a more advanced stage of ripening but not yet fully ripe (Commentary on the Mishnah, Uktzin 3:6).
shoots of zeradin and carobs. The tips of the tender branches and the tips of carobs at the time the trees bloom.
and of adal. Shoots of a vegetable similar to a radish.
the lof hashoteh. A kind of onion with broad leaves (Rabbenu Hai Gaon's commentary on Uktzin 3:4).
until they become sweet. Until they are made fit to eat by pickling (Commentary on the Mishnah, Shevi'it 7:5, Uktzin 3:4).
they become impure with the impurity of foods whether after they have become sweet or before they have become sweet. Since they are fit to eat even before pickling.
that he pickled them with their leaves. He pickled them in wine or vinegar together with their leaves.
for he pickled them not to eat them but for appearance. And anything not designated as food does not receive the impurity of foods.
the fine hair of kishut. The fine hair on the kishut (a kind of squash resembling a cucumber).
and its nets. The flower at its tip.
without intention. Without his having designated it for eating, since it is already considered food by itself.

once he crushes the combs it becomes impure as a liquid. Although honey is considered food while in the hive, it is not considered a liquid with respect to rendering susceptible (as above, halakhah 2) and with respect to impurity (for the impurity of liquids is more severe than that of foods, see Hilchot She'ar Avot HaTumot chapter 7) until the person crushes the combs in the hive and extracts the honey from them.

honey that flows from its hive becomes impure with the impurity of liquids; if he designated it for food, it becomes impure with the impurity of foods. Honey that flows from the hive on its own does not have the law of the other honey in the hive, which is like food, but is a liquid (Rashbam, Bava Batra 80a); and if he designated it for eating he removed it from the impurity of liquids to the impurity of foods (see Chasdei David, Taharot 2:5; Taz, Orach Chayim 158, subsection 7).
his intention is void. For it is not the way of people to use congealed oil for eating or drinking.

if he designated it for food it becomes impure with the impurity of foods. For congealed blood is considered food when one designates it (see Tosefta Keritot 2:19, that one who eats congealed blood is liable for the prohibition of eating blood).
milk that congealed etc.. See also below 9:2.

if part of it became impure, not all of it became impure. Only the place that touched the impurity, for snow is not considered one mass with respect to its impurity (unlike with respect to its purity, see below 2:23).
he passed it over an impure clay vessel. He put the snow into the cavity of the vessel.
all of it became impure. For an impure clay vessel makes impure all foods and liquids that enter its airspace (Hilchot Kelim 13:2).
the milk in the udder that he designated. Milk in the animal's udder that he designated for drinking while it was still absorbed in the udder (Gra's commentary on the Tosefta, Taharot 2:4).

his intention is void and it is pure. For the milk in the udder is not considered milk (see Hilchot Ma'achalot Asurot 9:12 regarding the prohibition of meat and milk), and even after it is squeezed out it does not become impure, since at the time he designated it, it was not a liquid at all (ibid.).
the milk in the stomach. Milk the animal nursed before it was slaughtered and that is still in its stomach; it, too, is not considered milk (see Hilchot Ma'achalot Asurot 9:15).

this becomes impure with the impurity of foods. Unlike the milk in the udder, the milk in the stomach is collected in one place, and therefore designation is effective for it (Gra's commentary, ibid.).
once the treader has walked on them in warp and woof. Walked in the winepress lengthwise and crosswise.
whole grapes. Grapes that have not been pressed.

once they are stored. Olives are stored in a vessel called a ma'aten in preparation for pressing, to soften them. From this point their work is complete and they are ready for pressing, and therefore the oil that comes out of them is considered a liquid (see Commentary on the Mishnah, Taharot 9:1 and below 11:6-13 regarding rendering susceptible). [Note: in some versions the reading is 'meshitanu', meaning beneath the beam of the olive press (and so Ra'avad read), but compare the reading in Hilchot Terumot 5:6 (according to accurate versions), and see further there in the Yalkut Shinuyei Nuschaot in the Frankel edition.]
orlah. Fruit of a fruit tree in the first three years after planting is forbidden for benefit (Hilchot Ma'achalot Asurot 10:9).
and kilei hakerem. Vegetables or grain sown beside vines or a vine planted beside vegetables, both of which are forbidden for benefit (ibid., halakhah 6; Hilchot Kil'ayim 5:7).

and an ox to be stoned that was slaughtered. An ox condemned to be stoned (for example, one that killed a person) is forbidden for benefit from the time its verdict is concluded (Hilchot Ma'achalot Asurot 4:22). And in the case where it was slaughtered, it becomes impure with the impurity of foods (whereas if it had been stoned it would be a carcass and would defile like a carcass).

and the heifer whose neck is broken, whether slaughtered or neck-broken. When a slain person is found on the road and it is not known who killed him, they measure the distance from him to the surrounding cities, and the elders of the nearest city bring a heifer and break its neck in a perennial stream for atonement (Hilchot Rotzeach 9:2-3). The heifer becomes forbidden for benefit from when it goes down to the stream (ibid. 10:6), and when slaughtered or neck-broken it defiles with the impurity of foods, since breaking its neck purifies it from carcass status like valid slaughter (Kesef Mishneh; see Hilchot She'ar Avot HaTumot 3:13).

and the birds of the leper. A leper who is being purified brings two birds; one of the birds is slaughtered over a vessel containing living water (Hilchot Tzara'at 11:1), and this bird becomes forbidden for benefit after its slaughter (ibid., halakhah 7).

and the firstborn of a donkey. The firstborn of a donkey must be redeemed with a lamb and given to a kohen. When the owner does not wish to redeem the donkey, its neck is broken and it is forbidden for benefit (Hilchot Bikkurim 12:4). The case here is where they did not break its neck but slaughtered it; in such a case it defiles with the impurity of foods as long as it is twitching, like any impure animal (see below 3:4, Hilchot She'ar Avot HaTumot 2:1; Kesef Mishneh in the name of Rashi, Bekhorot 9b, and see another explanation in Rashi there). It may also be explained that the case is where they broke its neck, and this breaking purifies it from carcass status (like the heifer whose neck is broken), and therefore it defiles with the impurity of foods (see Zecher Yeshayahu).
and meat in milk. Which is forbidden for benefit (Hilchot Ma'achalot Asurot 9:1).

and the flesh of a red heifer. From whose ashes those impure through a corpse are purified, and which is forbidden for benefit from when it was consecrated until it becomes ashes (see Hilchot Me'ilah 2:5; it becomes impure with the impurity of foods only if he designated it for eating, Hilchot She'ar Avot HaTumot 3:3).
and piggul and notar. Flesh of offerings that were disqualified (for their definitions see Hilchot Pesulei HaMukdashin 13:1-3), which are forbidden for benefit and require burning.
all of them become impure with the impurity of foods. All are considered foods with respect to impurity even though they are not permitted to eat.
a fig shoot that was cracked and hangs by the bark. A branch of a fig tree that was broken or cut but is still attached to the trunk by its bark.
all the foods on it become impure. The figs hanging on this branch can receive impurity, since they are considered detached.

and there is a doubt in the matter whether the rest of the tree is like a hand for this shoot that was broken or not. A 'hand' is something attached to food (such as the stem of a fruit used to hold it), and one who touches it is like one who touches the food itself with respect to receiving impurity (see below 5:1-2). The doubt here is whether the tree will become something like a 'hand' for the branch and the figs attached to it, so that if impurity touches the tree the figs become impure (for example, where they have already been rendered susceptible by liquids, as above 1:1).
that dried while attached to their parent. They dried while still attached.

do not become impure with the impurity of foods. Although attached foods that dried on their parent are considered detached (below, halakhah 5), these vegetables do not receive the impurity of foods because they are not fit to eat after they have dried (Bavli Chullin 127b).
he gathered them to dry them. He cut them while fresh in order to dry them (for example, for fuel or to make vessels from them).
they are foods as they were until they dry etc.. His intention to dry them does not remove them from the definition of foods, but they receive impurity until they actually dry.
twitching. Moving their limbs.

receive impurity. Slaughter makes them considered as if already dead and now food, and therefore they receive impurity even though they have not actually died yet (see also below 3:4, Hilchot She'ar Avot HaTumot 2:1).
a tereifah developed in them. If there is a sign in the fish indicating that they are inclined to die.
and they became impure while they were twitching. Impurity touched them while they were alive and moving.

there is a doubt whether they are considered dead etc.. Specifically with fish does this doubt exist; but an animal, beast or bird that became a tereifah does not receive impurity until it dies or is slaughtered.
the limb or the flesh hanging. That are about to be torn off but are still attached to the body.
that cannot live. These limbs cannot heal and reattach to the rest of the body.
if they were rendered susceptible. By one of the liquids that render susceptible to receiving impurity (as above 1:1-2).

receive impurity in place. Although they are attached to a living creature they are considered food and receive the impurity of foods (Riko, cited in Kesef Mishneh, Hilchot She'ar Avot HaTumot 2:5; but if the limb was torn off during its life it defiles as a limb from a living creature).
were rendered susceptible by slaughter. The blood that comes out in slaughter renders all the flesh susceptible to impurity (below, halakhah 7), and likewise renders the hanging limb susceptible.
like a hand for this limb. See explanation above, halakhah 2.
as will be explained. Below 5:3.

and there is a doubt in this matter whether the animal in its life etc.. Although after the animal is slaughtered it is considered a hand for the hanging limb, while the animal is alive the matter is in doubt, because it is a living creature and does not receive impurity (commentators on Bavli Chullin 128a).
in water in the ground. Water collected in a pit in the ground and the like.
kishut. A kind of squash resembling a cucumber.

that he planted in a flowerpot and it grew... does not receive impurity. For example, the pot has a hole, so that the kishut planted in it is considered attached to the ground (as explained below), and therefore the part projecting from it, though destined to be picked, is not considered detached and does not receive impurity (see Commentary on the Mishnah, Uktzin 2:9 and Responsa Radbaz 5:202).

that it is pierced enough for a small root to come out. It has a hole at the bottom of the thickness of a thin root that can connect to the ground through the hole, and therefore the plant growing in it is considered attached to the ground.
and likewise if there was water in it, it does not render susceptible. The water in the pot is considered attached to the ground and does not render other foods susceptible to impurity.
dung vessels. Made from cattle dung.
and earthen vessels. Made of dried earth that was not fired in a kiln.

do not render seeds susceptible. These vessels have no law of rendering susceptible (the seeds in them are not rendered susceptible, and the water in them also does not render susceptible), because the roots penetrate through them and they are considered ground, and the law of rendering susceptible applies only to what is detached (as above, halakhah 8; and specifically when these vessels are placed on the ground, Commentary on the Mishnah, Uktzin 2:10).
a flowerpot. That is not pierced.

is not considered a vessel. Since it is not considered a vessel, the seeds in it are not rendered susceptible, and the water in it also does not render susceptible (Commentary on the Mishnah, Uktzin 2:10, and as above, halakhah 8).
like a tablet with no rim. A flat board with no rim around it, so it is not a receptacle.
impure liquids that fell on foods made them impure even if they fell without the owners' consent. Unlike pure liquids, which render susceptible only if they fell with consent (above 1:2).

for impurity and rendering susceptible come together. Since impure liquids defile even without consent (below 10:5), they also render susceptible without consent (Commentary on the Mishnah, Makhshirin 1:1).
provided they are not in the ground. As explained above, halakhah 8.
in the way that it does not render susceptible. See above 1:2.
'which may be drunk'. This implies only a liquid fit for drinking.
the hide that he boiled. The hide of an animal or beast that is not fit to eat, which he cooked and made fit for eating.

and the afterbirth that he designated for eating etc.. Most people do not eat the afterbirth, but since some people eat it, it receives the impurity of foods when he designated it for eating (as below 3:2; Commentary on the Mishnah, Chullin 4:7; and see also Hilchot She'ar Avot HaTumot 1:15).
by themselves. Even when they contain no pieces of meat.
wheat in cattle dung and barley in animal dung that he gathered. He extracted whole grains of wheat and barley from the dung of cattle or other animals.

it became unfit for human consumption and is still fit for a dog, it is impure as it was. Unlike pure food, which does not receive the impurity of foods after it becomes unfit for human consumption (above, halakhah 14).
even for something whose seed does not decay. The seed does not decay in the ground but remains whole and from it a new plant grows (such as onion and garlic).
provided they take root. That the roots spread in the ground.
foods that are attached to vessels. For example, dough in the cracks of a vessel that serves the vessel (Rashi, Chullin 129a; and see Hilchot Kelim 20:9).
they have lost the status of food. Which receives only lesser impurity, and now their law is that of a vessel.

they become impure with the impurity of the vessel. If the vessel became impure with severe impurity (for example, it became impure through a corpse and became a primary source of impurity), they become impure like it, although foods never become a primary source of impurity (compare Hilchot Tumat Tzara'at 14:10).

for a liquid never leaves the status of a dog's fitness. Unlike impure food, which becomes pure after it becomes unfit for a dog (above, halakhah 18), a liquid never leaves its impurity since it does not become unfit for a dog, because a dog does not refrain from drinking a liquid in any condition, even when it is putrid (see Rambam LaAm and the supplements there).
for if he immersed impure water in a mikveh etc.. He put the water in a vessel and immersed the vessel in the water until the mikveh's water flowed over them.
and he immerses them: hot in cold and cold in hot, bad in good and good in bad. Although the impure water is not like the water in the mikveh, it is purified by it.
a reed full of impure liquids. A reed that was wet with impure liquids.
the water on part of it was not purified. The water on the other end of the reed, which did not enter the mikveh, was not purified by this immersion (and see below 7:5).
the temed. Water left to stand on grape pomace.
whether it became impure after he made temed of it. It became impure after he added the water to it.
before it turned sour. Before its fermentation was complete.
a pot. Made of clay.
such as honey and wine and the like. Which, when impure, are not purified by a mikveh.

and the first degree of impurity extended his hand and touched it. The case here is that he touched its inner part (since a clay vessel does not become impure from its back, Hilchot Tumat Met 6:3), and since he touched it from inside he also touched the liquids inside it.
this makes the liquids impure. For a first degree of impurity makes liquids impure (ibid. 5:7).
and the pot became impure from the liquids. For the Sages decreed that impure liquids make vessels impure even though they are offspring of impurity (Hilchot She'ar Avot HaTumot 7:1-2).
for a first degree of impurity never makes clay vessels impure. Therefore a person who is a first degree of impurity does not make the pot impure by touching it.
for a mikveh does not purify clay vessels. Hilchot Mikva'ot 1:3.
sewage water. Water that is poured out after use.
they are presumed impure. It is reasonable that they were used for impure things.

rainwater fell on them; if the rainwater was more than them, they are pure... whether in vessels or in the ground. When sewage water collected in the ground and rainwater was more than it, it is pure, like any water in the ground that is purified in this way (see below 15:2). But where the sewage water is in vessels, the commentators had difficulty explaining why the rainwater does not become impure from the sewage water (see the commentary of Ribamatz, cited in Responsa Ridbaz no. 15, Kesef Mishneh and others). In explanation, some answered that sewage water is not actually impure but the Sages decreed impurity on it because it is contemptible and people are not particular about it, and where rainwater was more than it they did not decree impurity (Responsa Ridbaz no. 1). Others explained that since rainwater does not fall into the sewage water willingly, as it mixes with it and becomes foul, the rainwater is considered attached and does not receive impurity, and therefore when it is more than the sewage water it nullifies it (Chazon Nachum and Mishnah Acharonah, Makhshirin 2:3; Chazon Ish, Makhshirin 4:2).
they defile in any amount. See below 4:2.
one who rinses. Washes.
and they drip. The water dripping from them after the rinsing or laundering is sewage water and is presumed impure.

and rain fell on them and the drips increased. The rain fell on the roof or garment and as a result the dripping drops became greater than they had been (Commentary on the Mishnah, Makhshirin 2:4, Kesef Mishneh).

if it was enough to anoint a small limb, it is pure as it was before. If a small amount of oil remained on the person, not more than enough to anoint the little finger of the hand, this oil is pure as it was originally. We do not say the oil became impure through the person and therefore is not purified by the mikveh, since such a small amount of oil is nullified as a minority relative to the person and is judged like the person (see Melechet Shlomo, Eduyot 4:6).

if he anointed with impure oil and immersed... if moist liquid remained of it, the oil remains in its impurity. If an amount of oil remained that can wet the palm of the hand, the oil is not nullified, since the oil was impure from the outset and is nullified only in a very small amount (see the reason in Ra'avad's commentary on that Mishnah, also cited in Tosafot Yom Tov).
and if not enough remained of it to moisten. That not enough oil remained to wet the palm of the hand (Mel'eches Ha'Aruch).
we already explained. Above 1:1.
and any food that is destined to make a person and vessels impure. Food that is destined to become a primary source of impurity (see examples below, halakhot 3-6).
pure fish and pure locusts. Fish and locusts that are permitted to eat.

the fat of a pure animal that died needs rendering susceptible and does not need designation. It needs rendering susceptible because it is not destined to make a person and vessels impure, since the fat of a pure animal that died does not defile like a carcass (Hilchot She'ar Avot HaTumot 1:5), and it does not need designation because it is designated for human consumption, like the rest of the body of a pure animal's carcass (below).

flesh that separates from a living creature, whether from a person etc.. Flesh from a living creature is not designated for human consumption and therefore needs designation, and it needs rendering susceptible because it does not make a person and vessels impure (see Hilchot Tumat Met 2:3 regarding flesh separated from a person, Hilchot She'ar Avot HaTumot 2:3 regarding flesh separated from an animal, and ibid. 3:10 regarding flesh separated from a bird).
and the carcass of an impure bird. Which is not destined to make a person and vessels impure (see ibid., halakhah 14).

and the fat of a pure animal slaughtered in the villages. In villages there are few people and much meat, and therefore they are not accustomed to eat the fat, so it needs designation there (Rashi and Meiri, Chullin 128a).

even though it was rendered susceptible by slaughter, it needs a second rendering susceptible after the designation. Although the fat was rendered susceptible by the blood that comes out in slaughter like the rest of the animal's flesh (as above 2:7), since it was not designated for eating at the time of slaughter, it needs a second rendering susceptible after they designated it for eating.
and all other wild vegetables etc.. Vegetables that are not sown in gardens and are not designated for human consumption.
shmarka'in. Thin, very sharp onion (Commentary on the Mishnah, ibid.).
and likewise locusts and small fish need designation in the villages. For villagers do not normally eat them.
olashin. The endive plant, whose leaves are fit for human consumption.
that he sowed for animals and then changed his mind for humans. He sowed them for animal fodder, and before he picked them he changed his mind to use them for human food.
for designation of attached produce. The intention he had regarding the food while it was attached to the ground.
need a second rendering susceptible after the designation. Since the first rendering susceptible was done before they were designated for human food (and see below 14:17).
the alal. Remnants of flesh stuck to the hide when it is flayed from the meat (Commentary on the Mishnah, Chullin 9:1).

and likewise the bones etc.. The items mentioned in this paragraph are parts of the body of an animal or bird that are not designated for human food by themselves, and therefore as long as he has not designated them for eating they do not receive impurity.

and the soft places of the horns and hooves. The soft places in the horns and hooves, from which blood would come out if cut from a living animal (Commentary on the Mishnah, Taharot 1:4 and elsewhere; Hilchot She'ar Avot HaTumot 1:7).
and the wings. The small feathers in the wings (Commentary on the Mishnah, ibid. 1:2).
and the down. The fine down that remains on the body after plucking the feathers (ibid.).
the beak. The beak.
and the carcass of a pure bird and the fat of an impure animal in the cities. For it is the custom of city dwellers to eat them, and therefore they do not need designation.

because they are destined to make a person and vessels impure at an olive's bulk. For an olive's bulk of the flesh of a carcass and of the fat of an impure animal makes a person and vessels impure (Hilchot She'ar Avot HaTumot 1:1, 1:5), and an olive's bulk of the flesh of a pure bird's carcass makes a person impure in the swallowing passage and makes garments and vessels impure (ibid. 3:1).
and whatever causes severe impurity does not need rendering susceptible. As above, halakhah 2.

the carcass of a pure bird in the villages. Villagers do not customarily eat it (for the reason see commentators on Bavli Bekhorot 10a), and it seems that the fat of an impure animal also needs designation in villages (as can be inferred from the preceding paragraph).

provided he designated less than an olive's bulk; but an olive's bulk is a primary source of impurity. For an olive's bulk of an animal's carcass is a primary source of impurity and does not need designation to receive impurity (and likewise the carcass of a pure bird does not need designation to defile in the swallowing passage, but with regard to the impurity of foods it appears that it needs designation even at an olive's bulk; see Hilchot She'ar Avot HaTumot 3:2).
an impure animal. An animal forbidden to eat.
and he slaughtered two in it. He slaughtered both organs (the windpipe and gullet), which is the measure of slaughter (Hilchot Shechitah 1:9).

it becomes impure with the impurity of foods as long as it twitches. Although as long as it twitches it is forbidden to eat even to a gentile, as a limb from a living animal (Hilchot She'ar Avot HaTumot 2:1; Hilchot Melachim 9:12), since the act of slaughter was done properly and by a Jew, it makes the flesh of the impure animal considered food with respect to the impurity of foods (Rashi, Chullin 117b, and as above 2:6; but after the animal fully dies it defiles as a carcass).
because it is destined to cause severe impurity. For a carcass makes a person and vessels impure.
he slaughtered one. He slaughtered only one organ, in which case the slaughter is invalid (ibid.).
or he nechara it. He killed it other than by slaughter.
it does not become impure with the impurity of foods. Since the animal was not slaughtered properly, it is not considered food until it fully dies (above 2:6).

and likewise a gentile who slaughtered a pure animal for a Jew... becomes impure with the impurity of foods as long as it twitches etc.. Although a gentile's slaughter produces a carcass (Hilchot Shechitah 4:11-12), with respect to the impurity of foods it is considered proper slaughter that makes the animal's flesh considered food as long as it twitches (and specifically for a pure animal, but for an impure animal a gentile's slaughter is not effective; see the reason in Rashi, Chullin 121b).
and it is like the other carcasses. After it dies it defiles by touch and by carrying.

one who cuts flesh from a limb of a living animal and afterward designated it needs rendering susceptible. Although a limb from a living animal defiles like a carcass, the flesh that separates from this limb is pure (Hilchot She'ar Avot HaTumot 2:3), and therefore if he designated it after he cut it, it needs rendering susceptible to receive the impurity of foods (like flesh separating directly from a living animal, above, halakhah 3).

if he designated it and afterward cut it, it does not need rendering susceptible etc.. Since he designated it for eating while it was attached to the limb, and at that stage it defiles like a carcass, which is severe impurity, even though after he cut it it no longer defiles with this impurity, it does not need rendering susceptible (see Yesh Nochalin, Chullin 9:10).

less than an olive's bulk of the carcass of an impure animal that he designated. For when it has an olive's bulk it is a primary source of impurity, but at less than that it needs designation to defile with the impurity of foods (above, end of halakhah 3).

and added to it other foods up to the size of an egg. He added other foods to less than an olive's bulk of carcass until all together they had the measure of an egg, which is the measure at which foods make others impure (see below 4:1).

since less than an olive's bulk that is within the egg etc.. Since if he added a bit more carcass and completed it to the measure of an olive's bulk, it would make a person and vessels impure, therefore the entire mixture is considered something destined to cause severe impurity and does not need rendering susceptible.
and likewise an olive's bulk of the carcass of an impure animal. Which defiles by touch and carrying.
since it does not defile by touch because of the dough. The dough wraps the entire olive's bulk of carcass so that it cannot be touched.

it needs designation. Although an olive's bulk of carcass is a primary source of impurity and does not need designation, in this case, since it cannot be touched, it needs designation in order to combine with the dough to the measure of an egg and make others impure with the impurity of foods.
less than an olive's bulk of the flesh of a corpse. Which does not defile at all.
for everything is nullified in the eyes of every person. People do not eat the flesh of a corpse (nor the food that touches it).

and the whole does not need rendering susceptible because of the corpse's flesh within it. Since if he completed the corpse's flesh to an olive's bulk it would cause severe impurity, the entire mixture does not need rendering susceptible (as above in the previous halakhah regarding a carcass).
everything becomes impure with severe impurity. For unlike the impurity of a carcass, corpse impurity breaks through the dough above and below (Bavli Keritot 21b; see Hilchot Tumat Met 7:5).

one who cuts flesh from a living person to feed it to a dog. He designated it for the dog's food, and this designation is ineffective for the impurity of foods, since the designation must be for human consumption (above, halakhah 1; and see below, halakhah 10).

if he designated it for human food, it needs designation and does not need rendering susceptible. If he changed his mind and now wants the flesh for human food, the flesh needs designation but does not need rendering susceptible. The commentators had difficulty explaining why it does not need rendering susceptible, when above, halakhah 3, it says that flesh separated from a living creature needs designation and rendering susceptible (see Merkevet HaMishneh and Arukh LaNer, Keritot 21a, who suggested explanations of Rambam's words; and Arukh HaShulchan HaAtid 164:18 and Chazon Ish, Uktzin 5:11 emended it: 'and needs rendering susceptible', but see Piskei VeShitot).

a young pigeon that fell into a winepress and died etc.. A young pigeon (a pure bird) that fell into a wine vat in the cities and died needs designation to receive the impurity of foods. And although the carcass of a pure bird needs designation only in villages (above, halakhah 3), in this case it needs designation everywhere since it was made repulsive by the wine in the vat and is not designated for human consumption (Commentary on the Mishnah, Taharot 8:6).
for they have action but no designation. See also below 13:4, 14:2.
even a sesame or mustard seed. A grain of sesame or mustard, which are extremely tiny.
or hands. For food that is a first degree of impurity makes the hands impure (Hilchot She'ar Avot HaTumot 8:1, and see ibid., halakhah 3).

and likewise one who eats impure foods is not disqualified until he eats an egg and a half. One who eats impure foods in this measure has his body disqualified and becomes a second degree of impurity (ibid. 8:10-11).
and this is half a peras. A peras (half a loaf of bread) is the measure of three eggs, and therefore half a peras is an egg and a half.
revi'it. A quarter of a log.
as we explained. Hilchot She'ar Avot HaTumot 8:10-11.
combine to disqualify the body at a revi'it. They combine to the measure of a revi'it to make impure the body of the person drinking them, which would disqualify terumah.
and the broth and the spices. That are cooked with the meat (Hilchot She'ar Avot HaTumot 1:7).

and the alal, even though he designated part of it and did not designate part. The alal needs designation to receive impurity (above 3:3), and although he designated only part of it, it receives impurity and combines to the measure of an egg and half a peras.

part of it a beast cast off and part of it a knife cast off. Which was cut from the rest of the flesh (and remained stuck to the hide), partly by an animal and partly by a person with a knife. Although the part cut by the person was separated deliberately from the rest of the flesh and the person gave it up, since part of it was cut by an animal and was not given up by the person, it receives impurity and combines to the measure of an egg and half a peras.
and the soft places of the horns and hooves etc.. See above 3:3 for explanation.

each of these becomes impure, makes impure, and combines to an egg or half a peras. When he designated these things for eating they are considered like other foods (above 3:3), and therefore they receive the impurity of foods, make other foods impure, and combine with each other or with the meat to the measure of an egg and half a peras (Commentary on the Mishnah, Chullin 9:1 and Taharot 1:2-3, R. Y. Kafih edition).
and they shrank. They contracted.
and likewise an olive's bulk of a corpse or carcass and a lentil's bulk of a creeping thing etc.. See also Hilchot She'ar Avot HaTumot 4:13.
an olive's bulk of fat, blood, notar and piggul. For which one is liable to karet for eating them.
that he put in the sun etc.. See also Hilchot Ma'achalot Asurot 14:4.

he put them in the rain and they swelled etc.. They swelled and thereby returned to the size they originally had (and this sentence refers to all those mentioned above from the beginning of halakhah 5).
whether for severe impurity. Such as a corpse, carcass and creeping thing, which are primary sources of impurity.
or for lesser impurity. Such as impure foods.
and sprouts of onions. Leaves that grow from onions and are not attached to the ground (Commentary on the Mishnah, Uktzin 2:9).
if they have moisture, they are measured as they are. The moisture inside them combines to the measure of an egg to make others impure.
bread of sfoganin. A sufganiya, whose dough is airy like a sponge.

the flesh of a calf that swelled and the flesh of an old animal that shrank. The flesh of a nursing calf swells when cooked, whereas the flesh of an old animal shrinks from cooking (Commentary on the Mishnah, Uktzin 2:9).
are measured as they are. According to their present size at the time they are measured.

the nut and the date and the almond that rattle etc.. They dried and a hollow formed inside them (so that they make a sound when shaken); although they were originally full, they are measured only as they are now and the hollow inside them does not combine (Rabbi Shimshon, Uktzin 2:8).

such as the flesh of a corpse and its decay. For the flesh of a corpse defiles at an olive's bulk and the decay of a corpse defiles at the measure of a full double handful (Hilchot Tumat Met 2:1, 2:11).
the flesh of a corpse and the flesh of a carcass. For a corpse defiles by touch, carrying and tent with seven-day impurity, whereas a carcass defiles only by touch and carrying with evening-impurity.

such as the flesh of a carcass and the flesh of a creeping thing. The flesh of a carcass defiles by touch and carrying and its measure is an olive's bulk, whereas a creeping thing defiles by touch only and its measure is a lentil's bulk.
a first food. That became impure from a primary source of impurity and is a first degree of impurity.
a second food. That became impure from a first degree of impurity and is a second degree of impurity.
that he mixed them. He mixed them together.

and if it touched terumah it disqualifies it. For terumah that touches a second degree of impurity becomes a third and is disqualified and does not make others impure (Hilchot She'ar Avot HaTumot 11:3, 11:7).
a fourth of sacred food. A sacred food that is a fourth degree of impurity (for there is a fourth degree of impurity only with sacred food).
everything is a first. Since the mixture contains the measure of the first-degree food that makes impure.
he divided them. Into two equal parts so that each has the measure of an egg.
each of them is a second. Since each of them is mixed from a first and a second, they defile as the lesser of the two.
they disqualified it. They made it a third degree of impurity.

if both fell at once they made it a second. Since the two of them together have the measure of an egg of a first degree of impurity, when both touch the loaf at once they make it a second degree of impurity (and terumah that touches it becomes a third).
they did not disqualify it. For a third degree of impurity does not disqualify terumah.
each of them is a first. Since in each portion there is an egg's bulk of first-degree food and an egg's bulk of second-degree food, they defile as a first (as above, halakhah 13).
each of them is a second. Since neither contains an egg's bulk of first-degree food but a mixture of first and second, they defile as the lesser of the two.
the soft branches adjacent to the food, by which the food hangs from the tree. Thin branches by which the food hangs and is connected to the tree.

like the stems of figs and pears. Figs and pears are attached to the tree by their stem, which is considered the hand of the food (and see below, halakhah 19, that the stems of figs are also considered a protector of the food).
and the end of the cluster. The end of a cluster of grapes outside the fruit that has no berries on it, which connects the cluster to the tree.
and likewise the pits and the like, of things that the food needs. See below, halakhah 13, in Piskei VeShitot.
for it protects it. So that it will last for a certain time (ibid.).

and the hand does not combine with the food to complete it to an egg or half a peras. For the hand is not considered the food itself, and therefore does not combine with it when it is impure to the measure of an egg to make others impure or the measure of half a peras to disqualify the person who eats it (as above 4:1).
for if the hand was rendered susceptible. It was wet by one of the liquids that render foods susceptible to impurity (above 1:1-2).
and there is a hand for less than an olive's bulk. The law of a hand applies even to something whose measure is less than an olive's bulk.
and there is a protector for less than a bean's bulk. The law of a protector applies even to something whose measure is less than a grain of fava bean (a kind of legume smaller than an olive).
and a protector that was divided does not combine with the food. Since the protector is divided into separate parts, it no longer protects the food, and therefore does not combine with it.
as people take out for sowing. The food receives impurity according to its condition when people sow it.

wheat in its hair. The thin husk of wheat is called hair (Dictionary of R. Tanchum HaYerushalmi, entry 'se'ar'; and in the Commentary on the Mishnah the reading is 'wheat in its husks,' following the reading in Bavli Chullin 118b).

and from where do we know that the hands of foods become impure... 'for all that is for your needs'. All hands that are needed and of help to the food, such as that one holds them while eating and the like, become impure and make impure when attached to it (see Commentary on the Mishnah, Uktzin 1:1).
one who harvests for the winepress. One who harvests grapes to make wine in the winepress.
has no hands. The stems connecting the grapes to the cluster are not considered a hand for the grapes.
because it absorbs the liquid. These stems absorb the wine and spoil it, and therefore he does not want them to remain (Rashi, Sukkah 13b).
one who cuts for shading. One who cuts branches with fruit on them in order to use them as covering for his booth (Sefat Emet, Sukkah 13b).

for he does not need the hand. Since he does not use the fruits for eating but for shading, he does not need a hold on the fruits, and therefore the branches do not have the law of a hand for impurity (ibid.).
that he trampled. He trod on and crushed them, and they can no longer serve as a hand.
a sprig of a cluster that he emptied. A thin branch coming out of the cluster that he emptied of the grapes hanging on it.
the shalbit of a date. The thin branch to which the dates are attached (below, halakhah 20).

an inner one, whether whole or cut, combines. Since it is fit for eating it is considered the food itself, and therefore it combines to the measure that defiles even when cut, that is, sliced (Rashi, Chullin 119b).

a middle one combines when whole; when cut it does not combine. The middle one is considered a protector, and therefore only when whole does it combine to the measure that defiles (see above, halakhah 3).
an outer one, either way, is pure. For there is no protector on top of a protector.
if he threw them away they do not become impure. They no longer serve as a protector, and are not considered food since people do not normally eat them.
if he gathered them for food they become impure. If he collected them for eating, he made them considered as food.
and if some food remained on them. A little of the food remained stuck to the peels.

even though they contain none of the cucumber itself, they become impure with the impurity of foods. The cucumber peels are completely fit to eat by themselves, and even if he threw them away they become impure.

barley, when dry, its husk combines with it, and when moist it does not combine. Barley husks are thick and are fit to eat only when dry and not when moist (Arukh HaShulchan HaAtid 167:7; and see Kesef Mishneh, who explained differently).
but wheat etc.. For the husk of wheat is thin and soft and fit to eat (Rashi, Menachot 70b).
all pits become impure and make impure but do not combine. They are considered a hand of the fruit (see above, halakhot 1-2).
except the pit of a moist date. The pit of a moist date, which is considered a protector and combines, since if it is removed from the date it will become repulsive and spoil.

the chotal on the pit of a moist date does not combine etc.. The chotal is the wrapping on the date pit that separates it from the fruit, and in a moist date the chotal does not protect the fruit and is not attached to it, unlike in a dry date.
part of which came out. To the outside of the fruit.
the flesh was on it on one side. The flesh does not surround the whole circumference of the bone.
we regard it as if it were the thickness of hyssop. Only a thin part of the bone, the thickness of a hyssop stalk, that is attached to the flesh combines (Commentary on the Mishnah, Uktzin 2:2).

for the bones are considered a protector for the flesh. Therefore they combine with the flesh just as the pit combines with the date (and this is where he did not designate them for eating, for if he designated them they are like other foods and receive impurity on their own, as above 3:3).
kulya. A closed bone with marrow inside it.
even like a bean. Even if the flesh on it is of the small measure of a grain of fava bean.

draws all of it to impurity. The entire bone combines with the flesh (Chasdei David, Uktzin 2:5). As to the reason, some explained that the marrow inside the kulya combines with the small amount of flesh on it, and therefore it draws the whole bone into impurity (Merkevet HaMishneh).
even though he boiled them for food. He cooked them for eating.
they do not become impure. Since they are not fit to eat even by cooking a lot (Chasdei David, Uktzin 2:10), and even as a hand or protector they do not defile since they are independent.
these become impure, make impure and combine. For they are considered a protector (see above, halakhah 2).
and the kaplotot. A kind of leek that grows in the Land of Israel (Commentary on the Mishnah, Uktzin 1:2).
and their pitma. The stalk at their top that gathers all the roots.
and the stem that is aligned with the food. The lower part of the stem of the inflorescence, which the food surrounds (commentary of Sfaray, ibid.).
the chazarim. Lettuce.
and the napus. A variety of radish (Commentary on the Mishnah, Kil'ayim 1:5); some identify it with turnip rape (from which canola oil is produced).
and its siv. The threads of the radish root.
the mintah. Mint.
and the pegam. A wild plant with a sharp smell and yellow flowers...
wild vegetables. Those that grow on their own in the field.
and garden vegetables. That are sown in a garden.
that he uprooted for planting. He uprooted them to plant elsewhere, so that he wants the roots to remain.
and the shizra of an ear. The spine of an ear of grain on which the kernels grow.
and its covering. The outer husk of the grain kernels (the chaff; but the inner husk, which is the bran, is considered part of the food; see Rashi, Chullin 117b).
and the kelisin. Rambam identified the kelisin as a kind of small fig (Commentary on the Mishnah, ibid. 1:6); some wrote that they are the fruits of the field jujube.
and the stem that is not aligned with the food. The upper part of the stem of the inflorescence that extends beyond the food.
a saw. A saw.
the pears and the krustemelin. Some identify them as different varieties of cultivated pear, and some identify them with plum and apricot.
and the perishin. Quinces.
and the uzrarin. A light-colored fruit resembling a small apple that grows on the thorny hawthorn bush.
kundas. Artichoke (and so the reading in some manuscripts: 'kanras').
a handbreadth on this side and a handbreadth on that side. A handbreadth of the branch to the right of the clusters and a handbreadth to their left.
and the tail of a cluster that he emptied. The lower part of the cluster that he emptied of the grapes on it.
and that are not normally harvested. Rather, they are uprooted and pulled by hand.
and the roots of cabbage stalks. Roots of large cabbages, which are cut off and thrown away.

and the chilfot of spinach and the chilfot of turnips, which are the stumps that remained in the ground etc.. Parts of the spinach or turnip that are not normally eaten and are left in the ground to grow again, and they sent out new leaves.
the pitma of a pomegranate. A protrusion at the base of the crown at the top of the pomegranate, which protects the seeds in the pomegranate.
and its nitz. Yellow stamens that form a covering over the pitma (Commentary on the Mishnah, Uktzin 2:3), and they do not protect the pomegranate seeds.
what remains is not joined to that which rotted. The rotten part is not considered a hand or protector for the rest of the fruit.
and what remains of the peel does not combine etc.. The peel over the rotten part, if it exists, does not combine, since its protection is not of use.
it is still joined to the food. For the peel is considered a protector of the food as long as it is attached to the fruit naturally (Commentary on the Mishnah, Uktzin 2:5).
until he crushes. He crushes the peel completely, in which case it is no longer considered attached to the fruit (ibid.).
megulgelet. Lightly cooked in hot water and still soft.
and sheluka. Cooked a lot and become hard (Commentary on the Mishnah, Uktzin 2:6, but see below, halakhah 7, in the explanation).

and if it was seasoned in its shell etc.. He seasoned it with spices while in its shell; it is convenient for him to keep the shell because the spice is stuck to it and he seasons the egg with it as he eats (Kesef Mishneh in the second explanation; Chasdei David, Uktzin 2:16).
a bone with marrow in it is a joining. Its law is like that of bones attached to flesh (above 4:4; and if it is closed it is a kulya, whose law was explained above 5:16).
even though he singed them with fire. In order to be able to pull them off the head easily.

they are a joining. Since the head is flayed separately from the rest of the body, the hairs on it are considered a joining to it because they serve it as a protector or hand (Chasdei David, Uktzin 2:16).
that he separated it. He broke the pomegranate apart by hand and thereby moved the seeds within its shell (Commentary on the Mishnah, Uktzin 2:6).
until he strikes it with a reed. Through striking the pomegranate's shell with a reed, he begins to actually separate the seeds from the shell.

are not a joining to one another. If impurity touched one of them, the others did not become impure, even though all are connected in the cluster (above 5:20; Gra's commentary on the Tosefta, Uktzin 1:2).
a cucumber that he cut... is a joining until he begins to separate. As long as he has not detached the slices from one another they are considered connected with respect to impurity.
a slice and everything that comes up with it is a joining. The slice that he takes, and the slices connected to it that are lifted together with it, are considered joined.
and the rest is not a joining. The other slices are not joined to the slice and to what came up with it (Riko, Kesef Mishneh).
the lower pika is a joining to itself and is not a joining to the slices. The rounded end of the cucumber is not normally eaten and therefore is not a joining to the other slices.
and he began. To separate.

the one he began with is a joining and the rest is not a joining... this half he began with is a joining and the rest is not a joining. The commentators had difficulty understanding this wording of the halakhah, and some therefore emended it according to the reading of Rabbi Shimshon and the Geonim in the Tosefta (Uktzin 2:14): 'the one he began with is not a joining and the rest is a joining,' meaning that the cucumber or half of it that he began to separate is not considered a joining since he is about to eat it, but the rest are considered a joining because he wants them to remain (Riko, Chazon Ish, Uktzin 2:13, and see Tosefta Rishonah, Uktzin p. 181; and see Kesef Mishneh, Chasdei David, Uktzin 2:14 and Arukh HaShulchan HaAtid 168:7-11, who worked to reconcile Rambam's reading without emending it).

even though he did not complete cutting and separating, it is not a joining. Even if he did not complete the cutting and detach the pieces from one another, they are not considered a joining, since one who cuts for cooking does not want the pieces joined to each other, as the cooking will separate them anyway (Commentary on the Mishnah, Uktzin 2:5).

to boil. It seems that, unlike above, halakhah 1, the meaning of 'boiling' here is partial cooking (Chazon Nachum, ibid.; and see Meiri, Nedarim 49a, that 'sheliqah' can be interpreted as partial or extensive cooking, all according to context; and according to the commentators who say that sheliqah is extensive cooking, some wrote here that, unlike ordinary cooking, boiling makes the food hard so that it does not fall apart; Tosafot Yom Tov and Tiferet Yisrael, Uktzin, ibid.).
this is a joining. For one who cuts for these purposes wants it to remain joined, so that it will be convenient to take out and arrange (Commentary on the Mishnah, ibid.).

any food that he has not yet separated is a joining, and if part of it became impure, all of it became impure. This is the division of the halakhah in the printed editions and in some manuscripts. However, it appears that the correct reading is that these words are the end of the sentence in the previous paragraph, as several commentators wrote and as it is in some manuscripts (see Yalkut Shinuyei Nuschaot in the Frankel edition).
food that was split and is attached a little in one place. Food that was divided but is still slightly connected in one place.
this is a joining. And both are impure to the same degree.
the other is like one touching the first that became impure. If the first piece became impure from a primary source of impurity and became a first degree, the piece touching it becomes a second.

this is a joining for a tevul yom, and needless to say for other impurities. There are things that are considered a joining only for other impurities and not for a tevul yom (see below chapter 8), but the leaf and the stalk are considered a joining to the food even for a tevul yom.
and likewise if it had a hand. For the definition of the hands of foods see above 5:1.
one may hold it by whichever of them he wishes. If the impure person holds one of them and the food comes up with it, the food became impure.

that he gathered them by their stems while soft and wove them all like a rope. He cut the nuts while fresh with their branches, and wove the branches together and made a rope from them (Rosh, Uktzin 2:5).
he began to separate the nuts and to peel the onions. He began to separate the nuts and onions one by one from the bunch (ibid.).
a braid of garlic. Heads of garlic that he braided together.
that liquids fell on. One of the seven liquids that render susceptible to impurity.
it is impure. It was rendered susceptible to impurity.

for a person's joining is not a joining for every matter. In this case the joining made by the person is not considered a joining, since garlic is braided when dry and does not bind well (unlike the previous halakhah, where the nuts and onions are moist and bind well, so their joining is a joining; Merkevet HaMishneh, Biur HaRadal on the Tosefta, Uktzin end of chapter 1, Or Sameach and others; and see Kesef Mishneh, who explained differently).
it is not a connection. Therefore, if impurity touches it (after it has been made susceptible by one of the seven liquids), only the place of contact becomes impure.
the dvelah. Dried figs.
they are not a connection. Things pressed together are not considered connected.
that he boiled them and they became one mass. He cooked them until they became a single lump.
that he piled them up. He heaped the olives to soften them (the place where they are heaped for this is called a 'ma'atan').

because from the outset he put them in the ma'atan only so that they would draw moisture from one another. The liquid that comes out of them joins them together, and therefore their law differs from other foods pressed together, which are not considered a connection even if they have become one body.

once he drove the peg into it, even though it has many lumps they are not a connection. From the moment he drove the peg in to turn them over, he shows that he does not want them to draw moisture from one another.

and if after he turned it over they became a mass, they are not a connection. Even though the olives became joined again after the turning, since he does not want them to draw moisture from each other, they are not a connection.
as we have explained. Above, halakhah 14.
it combines to the size of an egg to make other foods impure. For impure foods make others impure only when they have the volume of an egg (above 4:1).
and the lump on the other side is third-degree etc.. For example, where these lumps are terumah and sacrificial food, which have a third and a fourth degree.
and he made other loaves stick to it. He pressed other loaves against it until they stuck to one another.
all of them are first-degree. For the sticking joins the loaves to be considered as one regarding their degree of impurity.

it is third-degree, and all of them are pure, whether they separated or did not separate. Since a third-degree item in terumah is disqualified and does not make others impure (Hilchot She'ar Avot HaTumot 11:3), it does not make the other loaves third-degree, even through sticking (Arukh HaShulchan 168:26).
with impure liquids. Which are first-degree impurity.
with the hands. Which are second-degree impurity.
because they were one body at the time they became impure. Since they were joined when they became impure and all received the impurity together, they remain impure even after they separated.
the poured stream. A flow of liquid that is in the air while being poured from a higher place to a lower one.
one who pours. One who spills.
even onto a creeping creature. Which is a primary source of impurity.

the poured column is pure. The liquids that have not yet come down to the place of impurity are pure, even though the liquids below that touch it are impure, since the pouring column is not considered one body.
and needless to say, the liquids that he pours from are pure. The liquids above that have not yet begun to flow.
cold. Cold liquids.
and the vessel he pours from becomes impure through the liquids in it. For impure liquids that touch vessels make them impure by rabbinic decree (Hilchot She'ar Avot HaTumot 7:1-3).

because the cloud of hot vapor rises like columns of smoke and mixes with the poured stream etc.. The hot vapors rising from the boiling liquids below mix with the cold liquids in the poured column and in the vessel, and make them impure. But in the case of hot into hot, the poured stream is not a connection, since the influence of the lower is not noticeable on the upper (Commentary on the Mishnah, Makhshirin 5:10; it seems his intent is that the boiling heat of the upper liquids causes the vapors rising from below to be absorbed in the air and not mix with them - see Arukh HaShulchan 169:6-7).
and she stirred an impure pot. She stirred an impure cooked dish.
her hands become impure as if she touched the liquid in the pot. For impure liquids make the hands impure.
and she stirred a pot. And the pot is pure.
and her hands sweated, everything in the pot becomes impure etc.. For the vapors rising from the pot join the sweat on her hands to the liquid in the pot (Commentary on the Mishnah, Makhshirin 5:11).

honey of Zifim and honey of Tzafachat. Names of places whose honey is especially thick (Commentary on the Mishnah, Makhshirin 5:9). Some explain that 'zifim' is a species of bees (commentary of the Geonim there; Arukh, entry 'zef'), and 'tzafachat' is a food made of flour and honey (ibid., entry 'tzafachat'), or honey as it comes out of the hive mixed with wax (Tosafot, Nazir 50a).
because they have viscosity. When they are poured, strands like threads are drawn out of them, joining them into one unit.
as we have explained. Above, halakhot 1-2.
from stone vessels and the like. Vessels that do not receive impurity.
until the mikveh touches all of them from one side. That is, he puts the vessel into the mikveh, so that the water of the mikveh touches all the water in the vessel and purifies it.
as we have explained. Above, 2:21.
and likewise the sloping surface (katafras) that has a wetting liquid on it. A slanted place, like a slope, on which liquids were poured and some wetness remained ('wetting liquid').
it does not connect them to the other liquids on the slope. The liquids on the slope are not considered connected.
that are in the eshboran. A sunken place where the liquids rest in one spot (this includes also a vessel with water in it; see Commentary on the Mishnah, Tohorot 8:9).
a trough that is a katafras. A bowl that is placed on a slant.
and three pieces of impure food totaling an egg's volume. Three pieces of impure food that together have the measure of an egg (the measure for foods to make others impure, above 4:1).

they do not combine; if there were two, they do combine. Since a katafras is not a connection, each drop of liquid is considered by itself; therefore when three pieces lie one below the other, a single drop of liquid cannot touch all three together and become impure from them, unlike two pieces (A"R and Tiferet Yisrael, Tohorot 8:8).

and if beneath them there was standing liquid, even as little as a mustard seed etc.. When the vessel is not slanted and there is liquid at its bottom, even in a tiny amount, it combines the foods, by the law of liquids in an eshboran.
we have already explained. Hilchot She'ar Avot HaTumot 10:3.
there are things that are not a connection for a tevul yom even though they are a connection for all other impurities. As detailed below in chapter 8.
another person. Who is impure with another impurity.
a person who ate impure foods or drank impure liquids. He is second-degree impurity by rabbinic decree until he immerses (Hilchot She'ar Avot HaTumot 8:10).

barley and spelt when they are not hulled. Kernels of barley and spelt in their husks, which the Sages treated leniently, making them pure with regard to a tevul yom, since it is not usual to eat them like that except under pressure (Ma'aseh Oreg, Tevul Yom, general rule to chapter 1, mishnah 5).
all the handles of foods that are a connection for a primary source of impurity. The things that are considered handles of foods regarding other impurities (as detailed above in chapter 5).
are a connection for a tevul yom. For if a tevul yom touched the handles of terumah food, the terumah is disqualified (Rash, Tevul Yom 3:1).
any food that is split and poured out in part etc.. Above 6:9.

and anything that is not a connection for a tevul yom is a connection for the hands. Something that is not considered a connection regarding a tevul yom (though regarding other impurities it is considered a connection, as detailed below in chapter 8) is considered a connection when impure hands touched it.
and this too is a stringency of the impurity of the hands over a tevul yom. In Hilchot She'ar Avot HaTumot 10:5 the first stringency of the hands over a tevul yom was mentioned.
challot or loaves. That are disqualified by a tevul yom (such as challah of terumah).
and they were sticking to one another and he intends to separate them. They stuck to one another and he intends to pull one from the other.

who baked a challah on top of a challah in the oven and their surface had not yet formed a crust. The upper challah stuck to the top of the lower one before it hardened; he surely does not want this, as it spoils the shape of the bread (Commentary on the Mishnah, Tevul Yom 1:1).
and likewise water that was boiled and became like a dome. Water that boiled and raised round, hollow bubbles (resembling a tent), which touch terumah foods.
and split beans that boiled their first boiling. Split beans of terumah; their first boiling takes place while they are still clear, before the dish becomes thick and dense.
and new wine. Close to the time it was pressed from the grapes.
and they stuck and formed a crust in the oven. They stuck to one another after their surfaces formed a crust in the oven.
hollow. Empty inside.
and in the middle of the loaf is found something like a protruding nail. The dough that came out during baking now sticks out of the bread like a nail.
and was scorched during baking. Burned in the oven (in some versions the reading here is 'burned', and likewise below in halakhah 3).
and this is called charchur. From the verse 'and with fever and with the sword' (Deuteronomy 28:22), meaning heat and drying (Commentary on the Mishnah, Tevul Yom 1:3).
but a pebble in the loaf or a lupine. A small piece of pottery or a grain of the lupine plant that is put in a loaf to mark it (Commentary on the Mishnah, ibid. 1:4).
a wafer half of which was scorched. A thin baked item part of which was burned in the oven.
sacred meat on which the broth formed a crust, and a tevul yom touched the ladle. The broth floating on top of the meat congealed and the tevul yom touched it.

and likewise a dish of legumes that formed a crust over slices. Legumes that formed a crust over slices of bread (Commentary on the Mishnah, Tevul Yom 2:5); some explain that the slices are of legumes (Tiferet Yisrael, ibid.).
he disqualified only the stalk opposite it. For the egg is considered a connection to the vegetable, so the stalk opposite the touch of the tevul yom's hand is disqualified.
like a kind of hat. It overhangs the vegetable and is hollow underneath.
a strand of egg that formed a crust on the wall of a pan. A little of the egg congealed on the side of the pan and joined the terumah food inside the pan.
and a tevul yom touched it from the rim inward. The tevul yom touched the strand on the inner side of the pan.
its bottoms. Its base.
one who pours from one vessel to another. He pours terumah liquid from one vessel to another.
and a tevul yom touched the stream. In such a case only the place of his touch is affected, since the poured stream is not a connection (above 7:1).

he calculates the part he touched as one in a hundred etc.. Although impure terumah is forbidden to eat, if the rest of the liquid has a hundred parts against the part the tevul yom touched, everything is permitted.
as we have explained in Hilchot Terumot. 14:14.
he separates terumah from the pit. He separates terumah from the wine in the pit.
and a barrel of terumah fell from it and sank in a pit of wine. The barrel containing terumah wine fell into the pit of unconsecrated wine and sank in it with its mouth facing up.
from the rim outward is not a connection, and from the rim inward is a connection. Only if the tevul yom's hand entered the barrel from its rim inward is the terumah disqualified.
and if the pit was a pitas. If the wine container was not dug in the ground but was a vessel called a pitas, which is a very large barrel.

all of it is a connection, and if he touched part of the wine, he disqualified the terumah in the barrel at the bottom of the vessel. All the wine in the barrel and in the pitas is considered a connection, and if he touched even some of the wine, all the terumah is disqualified, even that at the bottom. The reason is that since the pitas and the barrel are both vessels, they are considered as one (Kesef Mishneh).

the fine flour of meal-offerings, the frankincense, the incense, and the coals. All these are sacred items that are disqualified by the touch of a tevul yom. Although the frankincense, incense and coals are not fit for eating, they were treated as stringently, because of their sanctity, as to receive impurity like sacred foods (Hilchot Issurei Mizbe'ach 6:8; Commentary on the Mishnah, Eduyot 8:1).

if a tevul yom touched part of them he disqualified all of them. Even though they are separate bodies, they are considered a connection because they are in a vessel, and a vessel joins what is inside it regarding the impurity of sacred items (Hilchot She'ar Avot HaTumot 12:7).

with the coals that he rakes into the firepan on Yom Kippur etc.. On Yom Kippur the High Priest rakes coals from the altar and enters the Sanctuary with the firepan; in this case all the coals are used, so they have sanctity and all are disqualified.
but coals that he rakes every day when he pours from a silver firepan to a gold one. See Hilchot Temidin U'Musafin 3:5.

have no sanctity, but he sweeps them into the channel. He sweeps them to the water channel in the Temple, from which we learn that the coals he rakes each day have no sanctity at all and are not disqualified by a tevul yom's touch (Kesef Mishneh, based on Jerusalem Talmud Chagigah 3:2; see Tosafot, Chagigah 23b citing R. Natronai Gaon). Some explain that before he pours the coals from the silver firepan into the gold one they do have sanctity and are disqualified (Raavad; see the commentary of R. Yitzchak in Tosafot there).
a mikpeh. A cooked dish.
and if he mixed. He mixed the oil into the dish or wafer until it was absorbed in them.
wherever the oil went, it disqualified. Even the dish or wafer, which are themselves unconsecrated, became disqualified because of the oil absorbed in them.
and a tevul yom touched it. The vegetable, after the terumah oil was absorbed in it.
that a tevul yom touched part of them. Part of the garlic or the oil.
he disqualified all of them. The entire dish.
if the garlic was the majority, we follow the majority. If there is more garlic than dish, the whole has the law of terumah, and if he touched part of it, everything is disqualified.
when they are a lump in the bowl. When the garlic crumbs are gathered in one place in the bowl together with the dish and the oil.
but if it was scattered in the mortar etc.. When garlic is being ground in a mortar it is not considered a connection, since he wants its crumbs to be scattered in the dish.
for their way is to be crushed in liquids. To grind them over a liquid dish.
if he crushed them without liquids and gathered them. He ground them over an empty bowl and pressed the crumbs together with his hands.
for they are like a round cake of figs. Even though he gathered the figs and made them one body, they are not considered a connection (above 6:14).
who designated the name of its challah in its north or in its south. He separated challah by speech, by assigning it a certain place in the dough.
kishut. A kind of squash resembling a cucumber.

its challah was taken from within it and returned into it, it is not a connection. Since the challah was separated from the dough and he is now particular about their mixing, it is not considered a connection to the dough (Gra's commentary on Tosefta Tevul Yom 2:1).
a dough that became mixed with terumah (nidma). It became a mixture, meaning unconsecrated produce with which terumah was mixed so that it is not nullified in it (see Hilchot Terumot 13:1-2).
or that was leavened with terumah sourdough. It was leavened by sour dough of terumah, and this dough has the law of a terumah mixture (ibid. 15:4; Hilchot Ma'achalot Asurot 16:1-2).

is not disqualified by a tevul yom. Although regarding eating this dough is considered terumah, forbidden to non-priests, regarding impurity it is considered unconsecrated and is not disqualified by a tevul yom (see also Hilchot She'ar Avot HaTumot 11:15).

dough that was made susceptible by liquids and kneaded with fruit juice. The wheat or flour was made susceptible to impurity by one of the seven liquids, but afterwards was kneaded with fruit juice (and this refers to dough that is disqualified by the touch of a tevul yom, such as terumah or challah).
he disqualified only the place of his touch. For fruit juice does not join foods into one.
defiled hands. Impure hands, which are second-degree impurity.

one may separate from it terumat ma'aser in purity etc.. Although terumat ma'aser is disqualified by second-degree impurity, since the hands touched the ma'aser before the terumat ma'aser was separated, it is not made impure by them.
because the first ma'aser is like unconsecrated food. Hilchot She'ar Avot HaTumot 11:15.
for a third-degree item in unconsecrated food is pure, as we have explained. Ibid. 11:2.
and she takes challah from it. She separates challah from the dough.

and she brings together the whole in order to take from what is brought together. She brings the vessel holding the challah close to the rest of the dough so that they are in one place, for only then is challah to be separated (Hilchot Bikkurim 5:13).
in a trough. A bowl.
a jug. A pitcher.

and said, 'This is terumat ma'aser for what is in the barrel, after dark'. He stipulated that the wine in the jug become terumat ma'aser for the wine in the barrel only after nightfall, when the jug will be pure.

the barrel broke before dark, the jug remains in its untithed state. Since the wine in the barrel was lost, the wine in the jug now has nothing to be separated for, so it does not become terumat ma'aser when evening comes, but remains ma'aser from which terumat ma'aser has not been separated, which is like tevel.

a tevul yom from corpse impurity or from relations with a niddah may work in the olive press. Even one impure from a corpse or one who had relations with a niddah, who were severely impure, after immersing may from the outset produce unconsecrated oil in the olive press, for they are now considered a tevul yom, who does not make even liquid impure.
they work with pure things. Which are neither terumah nor sacred items.

except the zav and the zavah on their seventh day etc.. The zav and zavah count seven clean days and immerse on the seventh day and become pure, and they are like a tevul yom until evening; if they see a discharge, they cancel the days of purification and must count anew, and even if they saw it on the seventh day after immersing, they become retroactively impure. Therefore it is forbidden for them to work in the olive press and handle pure things on this day, lest they retroactively make impure the pure things they handled.
as has been explained. Hilchot Metam'ei Mishkav U'Moshav 5:9.

oil or honey that became impure and afterwards congealed... are first-degree impurity forever. A change in their physical state does not change their impurity, and they remain first-degree impurity, like all liquids that became impure.

because they are like liquids, even though they congealed after they became impure. Oil and honey cannot congeal completely, and therefore they continue to be considered impure liquids (Commentary on the Mishnah, Tohorot 3:2; however, regarding receiving impurity in the first place, pure oil while congealed is neither food nor liquid and does not become impure, as above 1:19).
the gravy. Broth.
and the groats. A dish of beans.
and they require intention. They do not make things impure until he thinks of them as food (see also above 1:20 regarding milk).
and if a first-degree food or liquids touched them. A food that is first-degree impurity, or impure liquids (which are always first-degree).
they had on them a wetting liquid. Some moisture sufficient to wet a hand (Commentary on the Mishnah, Tohorot 3:1).
and they are primary-level impurity. First-degree impurity, like all liquids.

they are second-degree, like food that became impure through impure liquids. When they congealed and became food, they are considered as if they touched while still liquids, and food that becomes impure through liquids is second-degree.

if they were exactly an egg's volume, the liquid is pure. For foods make others impure only when they have the volume of an egg (above 4:1); when they are exactly an egg's volume, from the moment they begin to melt they fall short and do not make the drops that come out of them impure.
that were made susceptible. To receive impurity through liquids, but are now dry.

for the liquid is like something deposited in the food and as if it were one body. The liquid collected inside the olives and grapes is considered a separate entity, and therefore does not become impure when they become impure, and when it comes out the olives and grapes have fallen short of the egg measure and do not make it impure (see Kesef Mishneh and Ma'aseh Rokeach, who emended it to 'as if it were another body' similar to the Rambam's wording in Hilchot Issurei Mizbe'ach 6:7; and see Rabbi Shilat's note in Rambam Meduyak).
a zav, a zavah and the like. Who make a bed and seat impure.
and he did not touch the liquid. Even if the zav did not touch the liquid coming out of the berry.

for a zav who carried foods or liquids makes them impure, as we have explained. Hilchot Metam'ei Mishkav U'Moshav 6:5-6 (this impurity is called 'midaf', see ibid. halakhah 3; see Commentary on the Mishnah, Tohorot 3:3, and the commentary of the Rosh there, that the drop becomes impure by the zav's shifting).
pickled vegetables. Vegetables preserved in liquids.

it is impure and everything else is pure. Since the leaf outside the pot is considered separate from it, it does not make impure what is inside, even though part of it is in the pot (Commentary on the Mishnah, Tohorot 2:1).

it made the liquids in it impure, and the pot and all the pickled vegetables became impure. Second-degree foods make liquids impure, and these become first-degree and make impure the pot and the rest of the pickled vegetables.
and the liquid makes impure all the liquids in the pot and makes the pot impure. For the liquid on the leaf is joined to the liquids inside the pot (Commentary on the Mishnah, ibid.).
the vegetable is disqualified. Although this is only a doubt whether he touched it with his hand, it is disqualified, since a doubtful tevul yom disqualifies (Hilchot She'ar Avot HaTumot 10:5).

and the pot is pure. A tevul yom does not make liquids first-degree impure (and thus they do not make the pot impure), and even when the liquids are terumah he only disqualifies them (ibid. halakhah 3).

if it was whole and its stem had not been detached, the winepress is pure. Since it is whole, there are no impure liquids to make impure what is in the winepress (and as food it does not make impure, since a single berry lacks the egg measure that makes others impure).

and the grapes were prepared in a basket and the like for their treading. The grapes from which the impure person took this berry were placed in a container, which is the pit in which grapes are collected before treading (like the ma'atan for olives; Commentary on the Mishnah, Tohorot 10:4).

for he wants the liquid that comes out of them etc..
