By placing the grapes in the container, he showed that he wants the liquids coming out of them not to be lost, and therefore they are considered liquids regarding impurity (see also below 11:3). Therefore the drop of liquid coming from the berry without a stem, taken from the container and fallen into the winepress, makes impure everything in the winepress.
and he trod them in an empty place. In a vacant place with neither wine nor other grapes that could become impure from the grapes that fell.
as we have explained. Above, halakhah 2, that foods of exactly an egg's volume cannot make the liquid coming out of them impure.
and threw it into the oven and it was heated. Because of the heat of the fire, oil came out of the olives.
for foods do not make vessels impure. Even rabbinically (Hilchot She'ar Avot HaTumot 7:1).
and the liquid that comes out of them is pure, as we have explained. Above, halakhah 2.

for when one drop came out it became impure through an egg's volume and made the oven impure. Impure liquids make vessels impure, and even if the drop did not touch the oven it became impure, since the oven is an earthenware vessel that receives impurity from its airspace, even from impure liquids (Hilchot She'ar Avot HaTumot 7:3).

therefore if the impure olives were crumbs and not a lump etc.. When the olives are not gathered in one lump they do not combine to an egg's volume to make liquids impure (see above 6:16-17), and so the oven remains pure. [Note: in the manuscript there is a variant reading 'crumbs'.]
for he nullified them in the wood. Since the wood itself is pure, as it does not receive impurity, the impure liquids absorbed in it became pure.

even if he took out the wood so that rain would fall on it and it fell by his wish. Even when he took out this wood so that rain would fall on it, in which case the rainwater is considered liquid detached by wish regarding impurity (see below 13:2).

and he should heat them only with pure hands, a decree lest an impure person heat them etc.. Although liquids made impure by impure hands do not make vessels impure (Hilchot She'ar Avot HaTumot 7:2, 8:10), the Sages forbade this so that an impure person would not come to heat these wet logs and make the liquids on them impure, which would make the oven impure.
only the place of his touch is impure. For the dry olives in the mill do not make each other impure.
if there was flowing liquid. The oil flows in the channel of the mill and floods all the olives.
it is found on the leaves above the olives. The leaves with which the olives are covered, which do not receive impurity.

they ask the pressmen; if they said 'we did not touch', they are believed. The pressmen are the workers in the olive press, and although they are amei ha'aretz who are not expert in impurity and purity, they are believed to say they did not touch impurity (see also Hilchot Metam'ei Mishkav U'Moshav 13:2-3).
a mass of olives. Olives that all became one lump.
as we have explained. Above 6:16.
they were separate over separate ones and the liquid was below. Dry heaps of olives one on top of the other.
even if he touched an egg's volume, only the place of his touch is impure. The impurity does not spread through the whole heap when there are no liquids there.
an am ha'aretz. Who is presumed impure (Hilchot Metam'ei Mishkav U'Moshav 10:1).
a cluster and all its surroundings are impure. The cluster that the am ha'aretz touched, and the clusters directly touching that cluster.

the pomace and the grape skins. The olive waste and grape skins after the oil and wine were extracted from them; they themselves do not receive impurity (see above 1:11 regarding the skins, and Hiddushei Dinim, Tohorot 3:1 regarding the pomace).
that were made in purity. They were pressed by pure people and did not become impure.
these are pure, for from the beginning they were made in purity. The liquids that come out last are the remainder of the first liquids that came out in purity.

if there is between the liquids and the olives enough for them to wipe their feet on the ground. There is sufficient distance between the impure liquids and the olives for the pressmen's feet to dry off from the impure liquids.
for one who touches impure liquids not with his hand is pure. Since the pressmen touched the impure liquids only with their feet, they do not become impure from them.

all of them are first-degree impurity because of the liquid in the hollows, and the stickiness of sacred food, they are all like liquids that are not counted. Because the loaves and the liquids in them are sacred, they were strict to treat the loaves as the liquids in them regarding impurity: they are first-degree and make each other impure even if there are a hundred, for liquids are not counted as first, second and so on (Mishnat Eliyahu, Tohorot 1:9; Chazon Ish, Tohorot 1:16; see Hilchot She'ar Avot HaTumot 7:5).

only the third loaf is disqualified, and from the third onward it is pure. For a third-degree item in terumah is disqualified and does not make others impure (ibid. 11:3). Even the liquids in the loaf do not become impure from the loaf, which is third-degree, where the liquids are unconsecrated or terumah and not sacred (see ibid. halakhah 8).

and if there was a wetting liquid on all the loaves, even in terumah, all are impure and all are second-degree etc.. When the liquids touch all the loaves, all become impure from them and become second-degree, like foods that become impure through liquids, except the first loaf that touched the creeping creature, which is first-degree.

a bubble formed in the thickness of the barrel, like another vessel at its side. A hollow bubble that forms in an earthenware vessel while it is fired (Commentary on the Mishnah, Tevul Yom 2:8), attached to the wall of the barrel and appearing as a separate vessel.

and another hole was made to the outside, one opposite the other, or the inner hole was below and the outer above... all the liquids in the barrel became impure. When the bubble has holes on both sides in these ways, the liquids inside it are joined to the liquids inside the barrel, so if impurity touched the liquid in the bubble, the liquids in the barrel became impure.

the barrel was sealed with a tight-fitting cover and placed in a tent of a corpse... it became impure... for it is open to its airspace. An earthenware vessel covered with a tight-fitting cover ('tzamid patil') in a tent of a corpse does not become impure (Hilchot Tumat Met 21:1). But if the vessel has a hole it does become impure, and the tight cover does not save it from impurity (for the measure of the hole and its details see ibid. 22:3-9).

but if a primary source of impurity touched the bubble, the liquids in the barrel did not become impure, and they are as if separated from them. When the bubble has a hole in this way, the water inside it is not joined to the water in the barrel, so if impurity touched the liquids inside it, the liquids of the barrel did not become impure.
we have already explained. Above 1:1-4.
their derivatives are similar to them. As detailed below.
and the urine of human beings, both adults and children. Both the urine of adult humans and of children.
that melted. That dissolved and became like water.
the blood that drips at the time of slaughter. The blood that flows at the end of the slaughter when the slaughtered animal is already dead (Commentary on the Mishnah, Makhshirin 6:5).
but the blood of the spurt does not make susceptible, since they are still alive. For the spurting blood flows forcefully at the beginning of the slaughter before the life leaves.

and it is like the blood of a wound etc.. These bloods are not considered liquids, since the source from which we learned that blood is considered a liquid is the verse 'and drinks the blood of the slain' (Numbers 23:24), from which we learn that the blood must be such that the slaughtered animal becomes slain by its release (Meiri, Chullin 36a).
to the blood of bloodletting. Blood drawn in a medical procedure.

one who slaughters and blood spurted on foods and the blood was wiped off between one siman and the other etc.. The simanim are the windpipe and the gullet, by whose slaughter the animal becomes permitted. When the blood that spurted on the foods was wiped from them precisely at the moment between the slaughter of the first siman and the second, there is doubt as to their law: had the blood remained on the foods at the end of the slaughter it would have made them susceptible, since it is the blood of the slain, but where it was wiped off before the slaughter was completed, there is doubt whether it has the law of spurting blood or the blood of the slain (Meiri, ibid.).
therefore we suspend it; we neither eat nor burn. The terumah and sacred items that became impure on account of it are left without decision.
bloodletting blood of a person that he drew out for drinking. For the drinking of animals or humans, since by giving it importance it is considered a liquid (Rash, Makhshirin 6:8).
and the blood that comes out with the pus. The blood that comes with the pus in the skin or the phlegm in the throat (Commentary on the Mishnah, ibid. 6:7).
the excrement. Feces.
and the juice of meat. The blood that drains from the meat.

and the blood of a creeping creature, like its flesh, makes impure and does not make susceptible. The blood of a creeping creature is considered like its flesh, which is a primary source of impurity that makes impure in the amount of a lentil (see also Hilchot She'ar Avot HaTumot 4:7), and it does not make susceptible as a liquid.
and we have nothing similar to it. There is no other liquid that makes impure but does not make susceptible.
the whey. The liquids that remain after milk becomes cheese (Commentary on the Mishnah, Makhshirin 6:5).
as one who is unintentional. Without intent.
they make impure without being made susceptible. If they fell on foods, they make them impure even if the foods had not yet been made susceptible (see also above 2:13).
the discharge of a zav, his semen and his urine. And likewise the saliva of a zav, which is also a primary source of impurity (see Mishnah Makhshirin 6:6; Hilchot Metam'ei Mishkav U'Moshav 1:14).
and the blood of a niddah. The same applies to the blood of a zavah and of a woman after childbirth.
his plague. His blow.
along with the other derivatives of the water that come out of them. Those listed above in halakhah 2.
they make impure as impure liquids. All these are not primary sources of impurity but have the law of impure liquids, which are first-degree impurity (Hilchot Metam'ei Mishkav U'Moshav 1:16).

the oven and everything in it became impure. Impure liquids that fall into the airspace of an earthenware vessel make it impure and it becomes second-degree, and it makes impure foods and liquids of terumah and sacred items that are in it.
like the other pure liquids, which make susceptible only by wish. As above 1:2.
we have already explained. Hilchot She'ar Avot HaTumot 10:6.

and liquids that come out of an eight-month baby. An infant born after eight months of pregnancy is not considered a person but like a stone, and therefore the liquids coming out of it are not considered liquids (Commentary on the Mishnah, Makhshirin 6:7).

and one who drinks the waters of Tiberias and the like, even though they come out clean. The waters of Tiberias are laxative waters and they leave the body through the rectum, and therefore even when they come out clean they are considered excrement and are not considered liquid (ibid.).
one who drinks other liquids and they came out. One who drinks liquids other than water and they came out of his body from above (for example he vomited them).
they are liquids as they were etc.. If they were impure, they remained in their impurity, for impure liquids do not become pure while inside the body, but remain in their impurity, as below.
and he immersed. And the impure water becomes pure through the mikveh (above 2:21), even when inside the body (Commentary on the Mishnah, Mikva'ot 10:8).

or they spoiled and afterwards he vomited them, or they came out from below... they are pure. Although an impure liquid that spoiled and was ruined remains in its impurity (above, ibid.), it seems this does not apply to liquid that spoiled in the body or came out not in the usual way from the rectum, for this is mere excrement (see Hiddushei Dinim, Mikva'ot 1:8).

even though he immersed and afterwards vomited them, they are impure, because they are not purified in the body. Their absorption in the body does not purify them (and by the mikveh they are not purified in any case, above, ibid.).
we have already explained. Above, halakhah 7.
even if he drank impure liquids and sweated, his sweat is pure. The liquids that his body sweats are not the impure liquids he drank (Commentary on the Mishnah, Makhshirin 2:1).

but one who enters drawn water and sweated, his sweat is impure. One who enters drawn water with his head and most of his body becomes impure by rabbinic decree (Hilchot She'ar Avot HaTumot 9:1), and his sweat mixes with this water and is therefore impure (Commentary on the Mishnah, ibid.).
the sweat of houses, cisterns, caves and pits. Which are low places in the ground, whose way is to sweat.
even if they were impure. For example in a house with a plague.
but the sweat of a bathhouse is like water. For the sweat on the walls of the bathhouse comes from the water of the bathhouse.
and if the bathhouse was impure. If the bathhouse water is impure.

and he brought fruit into it, they became susceptible. Since it is known that anything entering a bathhouse necessarily sweats, the fruit he brought in sweated by his wish, and therefore their sweat makes them susceptible (Commentary on the Mishnah, Makhshirin 2:1).
the water on them is like detached by wish and makes susceptible. See below 12:3.

the dark liquid (mochal) is like oil. The black liquid that drains from olives is considered oil and makes susceptible like it (and see below 11:6-7 that when it comes out unintentionally and he does not want its preservation, it does not make susceptible).
liquids that drip from baskets of olives and grapes are not liquid. For they did not drip by wish and he does not want their preservation.
until he gathers them into a vessel. For then he considers them a liquid.
the wine in the pan. The wine that dripped from grapes being weighed and remained in the scale pan.

one who treads terumah grapes in a barrel, even though the wine floats on his hands. He put the grapes in the barrel to preserve them for eating, and pressed them down by hand in order to fit more in, until the liquid inside them came out.
the slaughterhouse in the Temple courtyard. The place where sacrifices are slaughtered in the Temple courtyard.
a law received by tradition. A traditional halakhah.
the blood of all sacrifices does not receive impurity and does not make susceptible. See also Hilchot Pesulei HaMukdashin 1:36.

sacrifices that were slaughtered in the courtyard are not made susceptible by the blood of slaughter. Unlike unconsecrated animals, which are made susceptible by the blood of their slaughter (above 2:7).
if the cow was muzzled outside Jerusalem. Its mouth was muzzled before it entered Jerusalem, so the needle swallowed in it certainly came from outside Jerusalem.
because it touched vessels found outside Jerusalem. The Sages decreed impurity on all vessels found anywhere outside Jerusalem (Hilchot She'ar Avot HaTumot 13:4-5).
in the contents of the stomach (peresh). Inside the animal's stomach.

the meat is pure. The needle does not touch the meat and does not make it impure, and the contents themselves neither make susceptible nor impure even when liquid, since it is a spoiled liquid (Commentary on the Mishnah, Eduyot 2:3).
as we have explained. Hilchot She'ar Avot HaTumot 8:6.
the stickiness of sacred food makes the meat susceptible. The sanctity and elevated status of the meat cause it to be made susceptible.
it is disqualified. It is invalid and forbidden to eat (but it is doubtful whether it makes others impure, Hilchot She'ar Avot HaTumot 12:14; see the Raavad's critique).
as we have explained. Ibid. 12:13.
to dry them. To make raisins of them.
until liquids fall on them by his wish, like other foods. As above 1:2.
to tread. To make wine of them in the winepress.
and he squeezes a cluster of grapes to test it and sprinkles it on the harvested grapes. Since he sprinkled on them by his wish, they became susceptible through it.
because he is not particular about it. He is not particular that the cluster's grapes be clean and whole, since he is harvesting for treading.
and he is particular about them that they not flow onto the ground. He is particular and wants the preservation of the wine coming out of the grapes.
for if he did not find a market for them. If he did not find buyers in the market.

they are not made susceptible until they come into the domain of the winepress. Even though when he did not find buyers the grapes are destined for treading, they are not made susceptible until they come into the domain of the winepress.

and likewise olives that came into the domain of the olive press are made susceptible, as will be explained. Olives picked to be sold in the market are not susceptible to impurity until liquids fall on them, but if he picked them for pressing in the olive press, they are susceptible once their work is finished and they are ready for pressing (below, halakhot 6, 8).

one who harvests grapes etc.. This refers to a case where the grapes were not made susceptible at harvest, for example he harvested them to eat or dry them and the like (Hiddushei Dinim, Tohorot 11:9).
or spread them on leaves. He spread the leaves on the ground and put the grapes on top of them.
in baskets. That have holes.
on a ground mat. They are spread directly on the ground.

and threw them into the winepress, and even though the wine splashes on the grapes they are not made susceptible. Since he harvested them for eating, it is reasonable that even what he threw into the winepress he still intends to eat if he wishes, and if not, they will be ready for treading with what is in the winepress, and therefore he is not interested in the splashing liquid and they were not made susceptible (Hiddushei Dinim, ibid.).

in a beit haperas. A field in which a grave was plowed; its dust makes impure by touch and carrying by rabbinic law, and therefore one walking on it with his feet becomes impure (see Hilchot Tumat Met 10:11).
and one who harvests for the winepress is made susceptible by their words. As above, halakhah 1.

he purifies the harvesters and the vessels, and sprinkles on them on the third and seventh day, and they wait for sunset. He must purify them like one impure from a corpse who requires sprinkling with the water of the red heifer ashes on the third and seventh days, and afterwards immersion and waiting for sunset.

to make it recognized that they are lenient regarding the impurity of a beit haperas only because it is a doubt. The reason they require purification of the harvesters and vessels from definite corpse impurity, though they are pure, is so it will be recognized that the leniency that the one harvesting in a beit haperas was not made susceptible is because this impurity is from doubt (see Hilchot She'ar Avot HaTumot 13:13).
and if these touched those, they are impure. If the pure harvesters outside the field touched the impure harvesters inside it, they became impure.
and they make them first-degree. For the impure harvesters are like one impure from a corpse, who is a primary source of impurity that makes those touching him first-degree.

for they were made susceptible once they left the beit haperas. From the moment the grapes left the beit haperas, the decree about one who harvests for the winepress applies to them and they were made susceptible.
for pickling. To pickle them for eating.

and likewise one who picks olives for treading in the olive press, they are not made susceptible etc.. Unlike one who harvests grapes for treading, who are made susceptible at harvest, for olives they did not decree that they are made susceptible at picking.
until their work is finished. Until their picking is finished and they are placed ready for treading (below, halakhah 8).
for the presumption is that they were made susceptible by their dark liquid. For the dark liquid that comes from them makes susceptible like oil (above 10:13).
for he wants its preservation so that they will be easy to tread. For the dark liquid softens them and makes them ready for treading.
only the place of their touch is impure, like all foods that were not made susceptible. For impure liquids make impure the place of their contact in foods even without susceptibility (as above 10:5).
pickled. Preserved.

he pierced it and the dregs plugged it. If after he pierced the barrel the hole was blocked by the thick lumps formed in the dark liquid (since it is not strained), so the dark liquid remained inside.
since their work is finished they are made susceptible. For the presumption is that they were made susceptible by their dark liquid (above, halakhah 6).

if he left them aside. He deliberately left a kav or two of olives outside the ma'atan (the place where olives are gathered) so he could add to them later and not need to keep his olives in purity (Tosefta Seder Taharot, p. 95).
but he is about to borrow and add. To borrow olives and join them to the ma'atan.

one who stores his olives in two houses etc.. Although when one stores all his olives at once they are not made susceptible until he finishes storing them completely (as in the previous halakhah), where he stores in two houses (two separate groups), once he finishes storing one of them, since its work is finished, the olives in it are made susceptible to impurity (see Tosefta Seder Taharot, ibid.).

provided he intended for them before he picked. That he intended to bring them down to the lower Galilee before he finished the picking, in which case their work is not finished until he brings them down there.

he finished his olives and is about to sell them, they are not made susceptible. Since he intends to sell them in the ma'atan, perhaps the buyer's intention is to add more olives to them, and therefore their work is not finished (Hiddushei Dinim, Tohorot 10:4; Gra's commentary there); others explain that since he intends to sell the olives, he does not want the liquid coming out of them (Rash, Tohorot 9:2, and as above, halakhah 6).

he is about to cover them with leaves, they are made susceptible. He wants to cover the olives in the ma'atan with leaves so they will be preserved in the meantime until the time of pressing (Hiddushei Dinim, Tohorot 10:4); even though he has not yet covered them, they are made susceptible since their work is finished (Gra's commentary on Tosefta Tohorot 10:2).

if there is a picker on the surface of the ground, they should be made in impurity, since this one is presumed to have finished. If the time for finishing the picking and bringing it to the olive press has arrived in the other places, we suspect that this gentile too has finished picking his olives, and therefore the olives were made susceptible and became impure through him, and they cannot be made in purity but only in impurity (Hiddushei Dinim, Tohorot 10:5).

and an am ha'aretz is believed to say 'I did not finish this ma'atan'. Unlike a gentile, a Jew is believed to say that he did not finish the work and his olives were not made susceptible, even if he is an am ha'aretz; though an am ha'aretz is not believed regarding pure things, he is believed to say that his foods were not made susceptible (see Hilchot Metam'ei Mishkav U'Moshav 10:1; below 16:2).
in a mortar. A pestle-bowl.
that they wait. That they soften.
they are not made susceptible, for his intention for them is for pickling. Olives destined for pickling are not made susceptible until liquids fall on them by wish (above, halakhah 6).
one who splits olives. He crushes them and softens them.
he disqualified them. For defiled hands are second-degree and disqualify terumah (Hilchot She'ar Avot HaTumot 8:2, 8:8).
for their splitting is the end of their work. For the purpose of softening is to prepare them for eating.
he split them to absorb salt. He split them so they would soften and the salt would stick to them, for salt does not stick to olives when they are hard (Rashi and Meiri, Shabbat 145a).
they were not made susceptible. For he is not interested in the liquid coming out of them.
and they reached the time for picking. And their time for picking had arrived.

they were not made susceptible. Because this liquid is little and is lost, so it is not considered a liquid (unlike grapes, which in this case are made susceptible because the liquid pressed from them is plentiful and is kept together with the grapes destined for treading, as above, halakhah 1).
to pick them individually and dry them. So they will be dried and fit for eating individually.

even if they are a cubit high they are not made susceptible. Even though they lie in a high, large heap so that the bottom olives stay wet, they are not made susceptible, since his intention is to dry them and he is not interested in the liquid on them.
that they soften. That they become soft.
that he will open them and spread them. That he will open the heap of olives and spread them on the roof to dry them.
these are made susceptible. For the liquid on them helps them to soften and he wants that.
until he guards his roof. Until he repairs his roof so it is a guarded place.

one who stores his olives in the domain of an am ha'aretz and locked and sealed it etc.. He stored his olives in the domain of an am ha'aretz and they were made susceptible to impurity. Although anything in the domain of an am ha'aretz is considered impure, where he placed the ma'atan in a closed place and locked it, his olives are still considered in his domain and pure (see Hilchot Metam'ei Mishkav U'Moshav, chapter 12).

even if he found the seal damaged and the key open, they are pure. For we assume the seal was damaged on its own (Hiddushei Dinim, Tohorot 10:6; and see also Hilchot Metam'ei Mishkav U'Moshav, ibid. halakhah 4).

if there were holes and cracks, he need not worry that perhaps he inserted a reed and shifted them. Even if the partition guarding the ma'atan has holes or cracks, there is no concern that the am ha'aretz inserted through them a reed or the like and moved the ma'atan with it and thus made it impure (for an am ha'aretz makes impure even in this way).
nidonot are like doors. And they need a seal on them.
and the eikel. A round basket made of ropes in which olives are piled during pressing in the olive press.
and those made of twigs and the like. Vessels made of palm leaves and the like.
and those of reed he leaves unused for twelve months. Vessels made of reed absorb a great deal of liquid, and therefore they must be left unused for twelve months until they dry in the air.
or he scalds them in hot water or in olive water. He soaks them in hot water or in the water in which olives were boiled.
a spring whose waters rush. Flowing with a constant, strong current.

and afterwards he immerses the vessels that require immersion. These actions were done to release the impure liquid from within the vessel, but the vessel itself, if it receives impurity, remains impure until purified by immersion in a mikveh.
words of tradition. Tradition of the Sages.

for it is a known thing that there is no seed that water has not come upon while it is attached etc.. Since this is so, it must certainly be said that an attached seed is not made susceptible, and the verse speaks only of seeds and foods that were uprooted from the ground.
and the liquids were detached. The water too must be detached from the ground (for the source from which this law is learned, see above 2:8).

any liquid that fell on the food initially by the owners' wish, even though its end is not by wish. For example, he wanted to wet the food with a little water, but in the end too much water fell there, not by his wish (according to Meiri, Chullin 16a); or he wet the food by wish, but after a time saw that the liquids were causing it to spoil and regretted what he did (Arukh HaShulchan 178:6).

or its end was by wish even though its beginning was not by wish. For example, at first he feared that too much water would fall on the food and did not want it to fall, but in the end it fell as needed (Meiri, ibid.); or it got wet not by his wish, but afterwards he saw that the liquids benefited the food (Arukh HaShulchan, ibid.).
one who puts his fruits in a river current to bring them with him. He floats the fruits so they flow with the river's current instead of carrying them in his hands.
one who leans a bowl against the wall so that it be washed. He leans the bowl on the wall so that the rain falling on it washes it.
he will be harmed. He will suffer a loss.

for a detached item that he attached for the matter of susceptibility is like detached etc.. The wall is something that was originally detached from the ground, and therefore although it was later attached to the ground, it is still considered detached regarding susceptibility, and the water poured on it by wish is considered detached.
one who bends down to drink. He bends to drink from the water in the ground.
one who fills the barrel. He draws water from the well with the barrel.

the water that comes up after it, and on the rope that is wound on its neck, and on the rope that is needed for it. The water on the back of the barrel on the outside, and on the rope wound around it, and on the part of the rope needed to sink it into the water so it fills (see the last mishnah of Makhshirin 4:1).
he placed it under the pipe etc.. It is possible to fill from the pipe without the barrel getting wet on the outside.

the water on him, even though it came down from the upper side to the lower, is pure. Rainwater does not receive impurity until it is detached by wish, and therefore even where it was detached on him and passed from place to place on his body or clothes, it does not receive impurity, since it is not by his wish.

provided that he shakes them off himself with all his strength. In order for the water to remain pure even after it separates from the impure person, the person must shake it off himself with all his strength all at once, so that it will not manage to touch him and become impure from him as it separates, for as it separates from him it becomes detached by wish, since he does not want it on his body (Commentary on the Mishnah, Makhshirin 4:2).
but if they were trickling and running down. That is, flowing and separating from him gently and slowly.
and when they are pure. In a case where the rainwater falls on a pure person who does not make it impure (Kesef Mishneh; and see Mirkevet HaMishneh, who explains differently).
and if he shook. He shook his body to remove the water on it (Commentary on the Mishnah, ibid.).
to bathe. To wash himself.
a barrel that was full of fruit and the leak came down into it. Raindrops leaking from the roof fell into the barrel.

even though he wants them to wait in it until he pours the water off them. He need not break the barrel in order to empty the water out quickly, but may wait until he pours the water from the fruit in the proper place for it (Commentary on the Mishnah, Makhshirin 4:4).
a trough. A bowl.
that the leak came down into. Not intentionally.

the water that splashes and floats above it is not detached by wish. The sparks that splash outward from the trough when the leak falls on it, and the water floating above it that spills from it when it is full, are not detached by wish, since they spilled from the trough on their own, not by a person (and all the more so the water in it is not by wish, since it collected there without his knowledge).

he picked it up to pour it out. As long as the water is in it, it is not by wish; but after he poured it outside it is detached by wish (like one who shakes rainwater off himself, where after it separates from him it is detached by wish, above halakhah 6; Mirkevet HaMishneh, above 11:1).

he left it so that the leak would come down into it; the splashes, the floating water and what is inside it are not detached by wish etc.. If he deliberately placed the trough so the leak would fall into it, as long as he has not picked up the trough the water in it is not detached by wish, because he does not want the water itself but only wants to collect it in one place so it does not soil the house (see Babylonian Talmud Shabbat 11b); but after he lifts it, it becomes detached by wish, even though he is going to pour it out.
for the water in his hands and on the fruit. The water that came up in his hands, which touches the fruit.
they are not made susceptible as long as they are in the water. For only detached water makes susceptible to impurity.
she raised it, any amount out of the water, it became impure by her touch. Since it was placed in the water by her wish, it is made susceptible by the water on it the moment it is detached with it.
a basket full of lupines placed in the mikveh. A basket full of lupines (a kind of legume) set in the mikveh (whose water is attached to the ground).

he extends his impure hand and takes lupines from it, and they are pure etc.. The lupines are in the mikveh not by his wish, and therefore they are not made susceptible by the water on them when he lifts them (as above, halakhah 10; Mishnat Eliyahu, Makhshirin 4:6; Arukh HaShulchan 179:28).

he lifted it from the water, those touching the basket are impure etc.. If he lifted the basket from the water together with the lupines, the water on the basket was detached by wish and makes the lupines touching it susceptible to impurity; and since the person is impure, the basket touching him becomes first-degree and the lupines touching it become second-degree. But the other lupines that do not touch the basket are pure, because the water on them was not detached by wish, so it does not make susceptible and they do not receive impurity (as above, halakhah 6; see Mishnat Eliyahu, Makhshirin 4:6).
one who fills with a kilon. A bucket used for drawing.
but after three days they are not detached by wish etc.. After this time he wants the kilon to dry, and he does not want the water remaining there (Commentary on the Mishnah, Makhshirin 4:9).
wood on which liquids fell by wish. And the liquids are still on them and have not been absorbed.
he took them out so that rain would fall on them. In this case the rain falling on the wood is considered by wish.

one who lowers the wheels and the cattle implements at the time of the east wind etc.. He lowers wooden cart wheels or plowing implements into the water in summer days, since wood cracks in summer and the water seals its cracks.
the water that comes up on its mouth is detached by wish, and on its feet is not as detached by wish. As above 12:4 regarding a person.
and at the time of going barefoot and threshing. When the animal suffers in its feet from much walking or threshing, and washing in water relieves its pain.

for they have action but no intention. Since there is no action here proving that the water that came up was by wish, it does not make susceptible (but had they rubbed the animal's feet in the water on purpose, this water would be detached by wish - Jerusalem Talmud Terumot 1:1; for this rule see also above 3:10 and below 14:2).

and likewise if his fellow pushed him to break him or to break his animal. His fellow threw him or his animal into the river to harm them. Or it means that he did it for exercise (R. Ch. Albeck, Makhshirin 5:1).
the first waters are nullified. The first waters that were on them by wish are nullified, and the water now on them is not by wish.
but if he pushed him in jest etc.. For he got wet by his wish and is not compelled in this (Commentary on the Mishnah, ibid.).
one who swims. One who swims.

and the water that comes up on him is detached by wish. This applies only when he swims for bathing or to practice and the like; but if he swims to cross the river from side to side, he is like one passing through water on his way, where the water on him is not by wish (above, halakhah 5; Mishnat Eliyahu, Makhshirin 5:2).

one who makes a bird in the water. He squirts water with a reed or the like for play and amusement (it is called a 'bird' because the water jumps from place to place like a hopping bird; some read 'pipe' after the instrument; see Mel'eket Shlomo, Makhshirin 5:2).
the splashes and what is in it are not detached by wish. For he is not interested in the water itself but only in the enjoyment of the game.
and if he measured its width... they are not detached by wish. Since it is possible to measure the width of the pit without getting wet.
and the water on the stone is not as detached. Since it is connected to the water of the pit, it has the same law as it (Commentary on the Mishnah, Makhshirin 5:5).
one who beats the skin. He beats with a stick the hide and wool attached to it, to shake off the water remaining on it after washing.
for his wish is that they come out. In such a case the water is considered detached by wish.
he beat it while it was in the water. To shake off the dirt while washing it in the water.

and in the eikel. The place where water that seeps through the cracks of a ship collects (Commentary on the Mishnah, Makhshirin 5:7; some explain it refers to the ship's anchor or the ship's foot or its rope; see Rosh there, Arukh entry 'ikel').
the kasya of tables. A cloth spread over food placed on the table to protect it from water and the like (Commentary on the Mishnah, ibid. 5:8; for other explanations see Raavad).
the cover of bricks. The covering spread over bricks to protect them from spoiling by water.
to temper it. So that it will be strengthened by the water and its cracks sealed.
the brand. A piece of wood that was burned in fire.

but one who takes out the nail and the brand to the rain to extinguish them, the water on them is not detached by wish. Since extinguishing can also be done by wind and the like, the water used to extinguish is not considered his wish (unlike tempering, which needs specifically water; and in making charcoal, water that extinguishes immediately has an advantage over wind, which takes time to extinguish and does not produce charcoal at once, and so the water is considered his wish; Hiddushei Dinim, Makhshirin 2:16).
the mashalet. A special vessel for drawing from water (Tosefta Seder Taharot, Makhshirin p. 114).
a jug. A pitcher.
he lowered the basket into the pit so that the hen would sit on it. He lowered the basket into the water pit to save the hen that was in it.
one who wipes the leek to remove the water on it. He wipes the leek forcefully of the rainwater that fell on it.

and the leek itself is made susceptible, for when they separate they make susceptible. The moment they separate from the leek and become detached by wish, they also make susceptible the leek they touch.

and if he removed the water from it with all his strength, it was not made susceptible. When he removed the water from the leek with all his strength at once, it did not manage to touch it while separating and make it susceptible (as above 12:6).
to shed impurity. To make fall the impurity lying between its branches.

and likewise if they splashed on the attached ones. It seems to explain that the water did not fall from the tree but splashed on fruit attached to it (see Tosefta Makhshirin 1:1 and the reading of the Rash there 1:4). Others explained that the water splashed on seeds attached to the ground, and they are not considered detached by wish because the seeds are attached to the ground and the water did not fall on them by wish (see Kesef Mishneh below, halakhah 16; Mirkevet HaMishneh above 11:1 and others).

one who shakes a tree and it fell on its fellow. He shook the tree and it fell on another tree, and from that second tree water fell on vegetables or seeds attached to the ground (Commentary on the Mishnah, Makhshirin 1:3).
or a branch (sukhah). A branch.

that water on the seeds and the vegetables is not detached by wish. Even though he shook the first tree so that the liquids would fall from it, since they did not come out of the tree he shook, they are not considered detached by wish.
terumah dregs on which he put water. Terumah wine dregs on which he put water to extract the wine remaining in them.
we have already explained in Terumot. Hilchot Terumot 11:13.
the first and second are forbidden to non-priests. If he extracted and extracted again, the water is forbidden to a non-priest because of the terumah wine mixed in it.

and of consecrated property for Temple maintenance, even the third is forbidden, and of altar sacrifices, forever forbidden. If the wine was consecrated for Temple needs, the dregs are forbidden even in the third extraction; and if the wine was consecrated for libations, their sanctity is more severe and they are forbidden forever (Hilchot Me'ilah 5:12).

and of definite second tithe, only the first is forbidden. In dregs of definite second tithe, the first liquid that comes out of the extraction is treated as second tithe, eaten in purity in Jerusalem, but the second is permitted as unconsecrated (but in second tithe of demai, which is obligatory only out of doubt, even the first liquid is permitted - Hilchot Ma'aser Sheni 3:12).

just as they said regarding their prohibition, so they said regarding their susceptibility. When the temed (the drink made from wine dregs) is no longer considered wine regarding prohibition, so it is not considered wine regarding susceptibility but has the law of water that must be detached by wish to make susceptible (Meiri, Bava Batra 97a).

for example, if they became temed on their own etc.. This law applies where the dregs mixed with water not through a person, for example rain fell on them and each time after the liquid formed an animal drank it, so that a second and third liquid was obtained and so on without a person's involvement.

for if a person was the one who removed the first waters... since he gave them importance and was particular about them, they make susceptible. Since he removed the first waters, he thought of the waters that would come, showing that they come there by his wish, and so they make susceptible like water detached by wish (ibid., and as above 13:2 regarding one who puts out wood for rain to fall on).
the leak. Rainwater that leaked from the roof.
and he mixed them so they would dry. He mixed the fruits so they would dry by distributing the water over all of them.
one who brings his fruit up to the roof because of insects. He spreads the fruit on the roof in the sun so that the insects in them will leave.

for they have action by Torah law. Therefore had they poured water on the fruit deliberately, the fruit would be made susceptible (Commentary on the Mishnah, Makhshirin 6:1, and as explained above 13:4).
and they have no intention, even by rabbinic law. See also above 3:10, Hilchot Kelim 2:1 and others.
they turned them. They turned the fruit from side to side so that all would be wetted by the dew that fell on them.
made susceptible. By rabbinic law.
the bundles. Of vegetables.
and the ketzu'ot. Dried figs.
so that they would last. So that they would keep a long time and not spoil (Commentary on the Mishnah, Makhshirin 6:2).
to grind. One who grinds.
if he was glad. That the rainwater cleans them.
they were made susceptible. Since he is glad that the seeds absorb, swell and look larger (Kesef Mishneh).
a barrel full of fruit that he put into liquids etc.. In a way that the barrel separates between the fruit inside it and the liquids outside it, or vice versa.
and they absorbed. The fruit absorbed from the liquids through the walls of the barrel, which is made of earthenware whose nature is to absorb liquids.
and in vinegar. Which is included in wine and makes foods susceptible.
but other liquids are not absorbed through earthenware. Because they are thick and dense.
one who takes out. He takes the bread out of the oven.

if it was wheat bread it was not made susceptible. For wheat bread does not absorb the wine in the barrel; for example, this bread was kneaded with fruit juice so that it was not made susceptible already when kneaded (Commentary on the Mishnah, Makhshirin 3:3).
because barley absorbs. Barley by nature absorbs more than wheat, and since the bread is hot it absorbs from the wine (for another law deriving from this see Hilchot Terumot 15:13).
one who sprinkles his house. He sprays or sprinkles water on the floor of the house so that dust does not rise.
and put wheat in it. After he finished sprinkling.
and became damp. They became moist.
because of the rock. Because of the rock-soil in the ground, which is naturally cold and moist.
in a trough. An earthenware bowl.
one who buries fruit in sand to make them wet, they are made susceptible. For example, where the sand is gathered in a vessel and not attached to the ground (Mishnat Eliyahu, Makhshirin 3:4).
in dry mud. Dry clay.
if it has a wetting liquid. An amount sufficient to wet a hand that touches it (Commentary on the Mishnah, Makhshirin 3:5).

he need not worry that perhaps his wheat was made susceptible if it became damp in it, even though he is glad. Although the person would be glad if the wheat became damp, he need not worry that the wheat became damp and was made susceptible; for unlike a house (above, halakhah 8), the threshing floor is extremely dry and the water is absorbed into it immediately, and there is no concern that the wheat became damp in it (Rosh, Makhshirin 3:5, cited in Kesef Mishneh).
and if he intended for this. That he deliberately gathered grasses wet with dew so that the wheat would become damp in them.
if there is a wetting liquid on them, they are impure. For impure liquids make susceptible and make impure even if they fell on the foods without wish (above 2:13).
and they went down from the upper side to the lower side, they were not made susceptible. See above 12:6.

one who blows on lentils to test whether they are good. He blows with his mouth on the lentils to check whether they become wet by it, for if they become wet it is a sign they are good and cook quickly (Commentary on the Mishnah, Makhshirin 1:6).
they were made susceptible by his breath because it is among the derivatives of water. See above 10:2.

and likewise one who eats sesame seeds with his finger etc.. His way is to first wet his finger with the saliva in his mouth and use it to make the sesame seeds he takes to eat stick (see Rash and Rosh there).
this liquid on the food is not by wish. The saliva on the food is not considered detached by wish, and it does not make susceptible the fruit that touches it.
split olives and fresh dates. Olives that are cracked so the oil comes out of them, or fresh dates.
to suck its pit. To suck the pit inside it.
the liquid on it is by wish. For the person eating these things gathers the saliva in his mouth and sucks it, thereby considering it a liquid detached by wish (compare below 15:7).

endives that he picked for animals etc.. The leaves of the endive plant are fit for human food, but when he sowed them for animals they do not receive impurity until he thinks of them as human food after they are detached (above 3:3).
we have already explained. Ibid.
water in vessels. Water gathered in vessels.
and it makes foods and vessels impure. By rabbinic law (see Hilchot She'ar Avot HaTumot, chapter 7).
pits, trenches and caves. Various kinds of excavations in the ground.
and gevaim waters. Water that gathered in hollows in the ground.

that do not have forty se'ah. The gathered water does not have the measure of forty se'ah, which is the measure of a purifying mikveh; and if it has this measure it does not receive impurity while in the ground.
whether they were not drawn or whether they were drawn. Whether they were poured there from a vessel or gathered naturally, such as from rainwater and the like.
or an impure person walked in them. In order to pass through, with intent only to cross from side to side and not to get wet in the water (see above 13:5).
these are pure. Since they are gathered in the ground, they become impure only by wish.
the one who drinks becomes impure. One who drinks impure water becomes second-degree in his body by rabbinic decree (Hilchot She'ar Avot HaTumot 8:10).
and tamtzit waters. Water drained from rains and floods and gathered in one place.
that have ceased. After the rains stopped falling and the floods stopped flowing (see Hilchot Mikva'ot 9:2).
even though they did not overflow. Even if they did not flood the pit to its end and spill out of it.
until most people walk. Until people begin to travel on the roads.
but in a geva from which it is impossible to drink except with great difficulty. Because it is deep and it is hard to reach the water.

until the footprint of a person or the hoofprints of a large animal is found recognizable in it. For then it is proven that a person went down there on foot, or riding on a large animal (Kesef Mishneh).
a small animal. On which it is not customary to ride.
for it is possible that it went down and drank. And it does not make the water impure.

the presumption of the mud and small hollows at the entrances of shops... they are pure. The water gathered in the mud and small hollows at shop entrances is presumed pure during the rains, like other water in the ground (above, halakhah 2).

the rains stopped, they are like spilled water, and those in the markets follow the majority. The mud and hollows in shops are mostly waste water, and so by default they are presumed impure (as above 2:26); but in the markets waste water is not so common, and so only if it is known that most of it is from impure waste water is it impure, and if not, pure (Arukh HaShulchan 183:13, based on commentators on the Tosefta; see Meiri, Mikva'ot ch. 1).

we follow the majority. If most of it is water, it has the law of water in the ground, which does not become impure and does not make impure except by wish; but if most of it is other liquids, it has the law of other liquids, which even in the ground become impure and make impure without wish.

oil fell into it; even if he congealed it, it becomes impure... for it is impossible to get out of the drops of oil. When oil fell into the geva, even if he removed it from the surface of the water, drops of oil remained there, and they are not nullified by the majority of water, and the whole geva has the law of oil. Unlike other liquids, oil by nature does not mix with water and therefore is not nullified in it (Rik"u).
it is one law. That they become impure and make impure even without wish.
tamtzit waters that have not ceased. When the rains are still falling or the floods are still flowing.
they are pure for every purpose. And it is permitted to use them even for terumah (Hilchot Mikva'ot 9:2).
one who was eating terumah with impure hands etc.. And the liquid made impure by the impure hands makes the terumah impure (see Hilchot She'ar Avot HaTumot 8:8).
a dvelah. A dried fig.
to remove a pebble. To take out of his mouth a stone or the like.
if he turned. His finger in his mouth (Commentary on the Mishnah, Kelim 8:10), and thereby uprooted the saliva from its place.
the dvelah became impure through his saliva. For saliva is considered a liquid (above 10:2), and since it became impure it makes the dvelah susceptible and impure at once (as above 2:13).
or he sucks it to remove it. He gathers the saliva and sucks it before taking it out of his mouth.
as we have explained. Above, halakhah 1.
a pundion. A kind of coin.

if he put it in for his thirst. He put the pundion in his mouth so that his saliva would gather on it and thereby quench his thirst (Commentary on the Mishnah, Kelim 8:10; see Hilchot Rotze'ach 12:4, that this is forbidden because of danger).
and she was sweeping out the impure oven. She was removing ashes from the impure oven; the oven is an earthenware vessel and makes impure whatever enters its airspace.
the terumah in her mouth became impure. Her hand became impure from the oven and made her saliva impure, and it makes the terumah foods impure.
all the bundles in the markets. Bundles of vegetables sold in markets.
because their way. Of the sellers.
and flour and fine flour, they soak it. Before grinding, they soak the wheat in water to clean it.
pot dishes such as ripot and the like. Which are kinds of ground grain boiled in a pot.

they are presumed to be made susceptible everywhere, whether those of the markets or those of houses etc.. Unlike flour and fine flour, where only that sold in the market is presumed susceptible because it was certainly soaked before grinding to be clean (not so in other places that are not particular about this, see Babylonian Talmud Pesachim 40a), in pot dishes even that found in houses is presumed susceptible, since everyone soaks them to remove their husks (Arukh HaShulchan 184:1; Chazon Ish, Makhshirin 6:8; see also Rashi, Mo'ed Katan 13b).

and regarding all of them an am ha'aretz is believed to say they were not made susceptible etc.. Although an am ha'aretz is not believed regarding pure things (Hilchot Metam'ei Mishkav U'Moshav 10:1), he is believed to say about fruit that it was not made susceptible, even about those presumed susceptible.
whether he caught them with a net (cherem), or with a seine (yakhpuf), or with a trap (metzudah). Different kinds of nets and fishing nets.

if he did not shake the trap over them, they were not made susceptible, and if he shook, they were made susceptible. For the water in traps and nets is not considered detached by wish until they are shaken (above 13:11).

and an am ha'aretz is not believed to say 'I did not shake the trap over them'. For fishermen are not careful not to shake the trap over the fish, because they think they were already made susceptible by the water on them, and they do not know that attached water does not make susceptible until detached by wish (Rosh, Makhshirin 6:3).

all tzir is presumed susceptible. Tzir is the brine that drains from salted fish or locusts, and it is usually mixed with water or other liquids, and therefore it is presumed susceptible (Commentary on the Mishnah, Makhshirin 6:3).

pure tzir into which any amount of water fell, the whole is a liquid and makes susceptible etc.. Tzir that is known to contain no liquid at all, for example that was pickled with salt only or with fruit juice, if a drop of water fell into it the whole becomes liquid and makes susceptible and can become impure (Commentary on the Mishnah, Makhshirin 6:3).

and the tzir of impure locusts does not make susceptible but becomes impure with the impurity of liquids. It is not considered a liquid (because of the liquid mixed in it) regarding susceptibility but only regarding impurity.
he touches it to water and it is pure. See above 2:21, 2:24.

and the water in it was nullified by its smallness. Unlike water that falls into tzir after it has formed, where even one drop makes it a liquid (above, halakhah 4), the water in which fish are pickled to extract tzir from them is nullified by the majority of the fluid coming out of the fish and has the law of the tzir itself (Or Sameach, Hilchot Bikkurim 6:12).

but into a pot, kind meets its kind and awakens etc.. When this tzir is put into a pot, the water in it meets the water in the pot and becomes the majority and is no longer nullified, and it makes impure all the water in the pot (for the water that was in the tzir was not purified in the mikveh, because as it was a minority of the tzir, the touching did not help to purify it).
the og. A plant with red clusters, from which the spice sumac is made (see Commentary on the Mishnah, Demai 1:1).

in the presumption of impurity. Since its way is to shrivel and dry, it is customary to sprinkle water on it (Hiddushei Dinim, Makhshirin 3:9), and since it is presumed susceptible it is also presumed impure (as above, halakhah 2).
and likewise all the hanging cucumbers and gourds etc.. For they hang a long time and water is sprinkled on them to keep them moist (Hiddushei Dinim, ibid.).
if so, why was it said that the first-degree in unconsecrated food is impure etc.. Since there is no prohibition to eat impure unconsecrated food, why do we count the degrees of impurity in it.
as we have explained. Hilchot She'ar Avot HaTumot 11:2-4, 11:7.

and likewise one who eats second-degree unconsecrated food, if he touches terumah he disqualifies it. One who eats impure foods becomes second-degree in his body and disqualifies terumah by his touch (ibid. 8:10).

and one may make impure the prepared unconsecrated produce. It is permitted to make unconsecrated produce impure after terumot and ma'aserot have been separated from it (but it is forbidden to make terumah impure, see Hilchot Terumot 12:1).
on every festival. On each of the three pilgrimage festivals.
he does not receive lashes. The forty lashes.
the impure and the pure together. The verse was said regarding eating the meat of unconsecrated animals (and likewise eating a blemished firstborn, which has the law of unconsecrated).
from the oral tradition. The tradition of the Sages in explaining the verses.
they eat from one bowl. From the same dish. And we do not worry that the impure one will make impure the food the pure one eats or the pure one himself, for they were not warned about this.
as we have explained. Hilchot Ishut 21:8, Hilchot Issurei Bi'ah 11:18-19.
and a zav shall not eat with a zavah. Even though both are impure.
and purity of the body brings to sanctity of the soul etc.. See Hilchot Mikva'ot 11:12, and see also Hilchot Ma'achalot Asurot 17:32.
bad character traits. Bad traits.
